Artifact_Name: Communication Radio — AN/PRC-25 Field Radio
Description: An American AN/PRC-25 VHF frequency-modulated infantry radio used by Forward Air Controllers (FACs) during the 1971 Liberation War. Forward air controllers were army officers posted with ground forces who directed air strikes by radio, providing targeting information to attacking aircraft. The PRC-25 operates on FM frequencies in the 30–75.95 MHz band and has a range of approximately 5–8 km. This example was used to coordinate Hawker Hunter close air support strikes during the liberation campaign. The radio is displayed with its original carrying harness, handset, and antenna, alongside a photograph of a FAC team at work.

Artifact_Name: Scale Model Collection — BAF Aircraft Fleet (1971–2000)
Description: A cabinet display of precision scale models of every aircraft type that served in the Bangladesh Air Force from its founding in 1971 to the turn of the millennium. The collection includes: Hawker Hunter FGA.9, de Havilland Vampire, MiG-21 MF, Shenyang F-6, Cessna T-37, Aermacchi MB-339, Fouga Magister, Mil Mi-8, Bell 212, and An-24 transport. Each model is detailed to 1:48 or 1:72 scale and painted in the exact livery worn during BAF service, including the national roundel, serial numbers, and tactical markings. The accompanying labels give the service dates, primary roles, and key technical specifications of each aircraft.

Artifact_Name: Antonov An-24 Transport Aircraft
Description: The Antonov An-24 is a Soviet twin-turboprop short-haul transport and passenger aircraft used by the Bangladesh Air Force for VIP transport, logistics, and military airlift. Bangladesh acquired An-24s from the Soviet Union in the early years after independence. The aircraft can carry up to 50 passengers or equivalent cargo and operates from unpaved runways — a critical requirement for Bangladesh's limited airfield infrastructure in the 1970s. The An-24 served both military and quasi-civilian government transport roles. This museum example is one of the best-preserved Soviet-era transport aircraft in Bangladesh and represents the Soviet Union's significant contribution to BAF's early capability.

Artifact_Name: Medals Display — Liberation War and Service Awards
Description: A display case of medals awarded to Bangladesh Air Force officers and airmen, including: the Bir Uttom (second highest gallantry award) awarded to pilots who flew combat missions in 1971; the Bangladesh Muktijoddha Padak (Liberation War Medal); service medals for UN peacekeeping deployments in Cambodia, Somalia, and Sierra Leone; and long service awards. The medals are displayed on black velvet with printed labels identifying the recipient, date of award, and the action or service for which the decoration was given. This display humanises the institutional history of the BAF through the individual stories of its members' distinguished service.

Artifact_Name: Parachute and Survival Equipment Display
Description: A comprehensive display of parachute and aircrew survival equipment used by BAF pilots. The exhibit includes a back-type pilot parachute (the type used in non-ejection-seat aircraft), a seat-type parachute harness, and a personal survival pack containing: first-aid kit, waterproof matches, compass, signalling mirror, emergency rations, water purification tablets, and a survival knife. An instructional panel explains how to correctly don and operate a parachute and the correct emergency landing procedure. The equipment reflects the serious operational planning that underlies peacetime military aviation, preparing for the possibility of an aircraft emergency.

Artifact_Name: BAF Museum Main Hall Diorama — Liberation War Air Operations
Provenance_Note: Bangladesh Air Force Museum curatorial team
Description: A large three-dimensional diorama depicting the air operations of the Bangladesh Air Force and the Indian Air Force during the December 1971 war. The diorama shows a map of Bangladesh with forward air bases, target locations, and attack routes rendered in three dimensions. Miniature aircraft on wire supports represent BAF and IAF sorties. Red stars on the map indicate Pakistani installations that were struck. An audio commentary (looped) narrates the sequence of air operations from the beginning of the Indian Air Force's air campaign on 3 December 1971 to the fall of Dhaka on 16 December. This is one of the most popular exhibits in the museum, particularly for school children.

Artifact_Name: Crash Remains — Pakistani Aircraft (1971)
Provenance_Note: Recovered by Bangladesh Air Force and Army
Description: Wreckage fragments and recovered components from Pakistani Air Force aircraft shot down or destroyed during the 1971 Liberation War. The display includes: a section of wing skin with bullet holes, an instrument panel recovered from a crashed Sabre jet, and a partially intact engine cowling. Labels identify the aircraft type, the location where wreckage was found, and the engagement in which the aircraft was lost. These physical remains of destroyed enemy aircraft are among the most viscerally powerful exhibits in the museum, tangible evidence of the air battles that contributed to Bangladesh's liberation.

Artifact_Name: Visitor's Book — 1977 to Present
Description: The official visitor's book of the Bangladesh Air Force Museum, maintained since the museum's opening in 1977. The book contains signatures, comments, and messages from notable visitors including Heads of State, foreign dignitaries, senior military officers, veterans of the 1971 Liberation War, and ordinary Bangladeshi citizens. Selected pages from the book are displayed in a glass case, including entries from early visitors in 1977, entries from Liberation War veterans, and comments from international guests. The visitor's book is a social history of the museum and of Bangladesh's engagement with its own military heritage.

Artifact_Name: Nakshi Kantha — Embroidered Quilt
Description: A traditional nakshi kantha (embroidered quilt) made from layers of old sari cloth stitched together with colorful thread. The surface is covered with intricate patterns depicting rural life, birds, flowers, and geometric motifs. Nakshi kanthas are a quintessential Bengali folk art, traditionally made by women in rural homes. This example comes from Jamalpur district, a region renowned for the finest kantha work. The central panel shows a tree of life flanked by peacocks and surrounded by a border of lotus flowers.

Artifact_Name: Traditional Wooden Puppet (Putool)
Description: A hand-carved wooden puppet (putool) used in traditional Bengali puppet theatre (putool nach). The figure represents a village maiden in a red sari with painted features and articulated limbs controlled by strings. Puppet theatre has been a beloved form of entertainment and moral storytelling for children in Bangladesh for centuries, conveying folk tales and epics like the Ramayana. This puppet originates from Sylhet, where a distinct style of puppetry flourished.

Artifact_Name: Clay Doll of Rajshahi (Mati Putul)
Description: A painted clay doll (mati putul) from Rajshahi, depicting a woman carrying a water pot on her head. Made from fine alluvial clay, fired in a traditional kiln, and painted with natural mineral pigments in red, white, and black. Clay dolls have been made in Bangladesh for thousands of years and remain a vital folk industry. The Rajshahi style is distinguished by its elongated proportions and geometric facial features. Such dolls were traditionally sold at rural fairs and used both as toys and as household decorations.

Artifact_Name: Hand-painted Rickshaw Panel
Description: A hand-painted decorative panel from the back of a Dhaka rickshaw, depicting a Bengali landscape scene: a river with boats, coconut palms, and a village at sunset. Rickshaw art is a uniquely Bangladeshi form of urban folk painting, developed in Dhaka from the 1940s onward. Each panel is individually painted by specialized artists using bright enamel paints on sheet metal. These vivid images — combining nature scenes, film stars, tigers, and national symbols — have become a defining visual identity of Bangladesh's capital.

Artifact_Name: Manuscript of Bengali Nursery Rhymes (Chhara Sangkalan)
Description: A handwritten compilation of traditional Bengali nursery rhymes and children's songs (chhara), collected and transcribed in the 1940s. The manuscript includes over 50 traditional rhymes including verses about seasons, animals, rivers, and village life. Many of these rhymes are attributed to anonymous rural poets and have been passed down orally for generations. The collection was assembled by a Dhaka schoolteacher as part of an effort to preserve children's oral literature during the tumultuous years of the Partition. It represents an irreplaceable document of Bengal's intangible cultural heritage.

Artifact_Name: Bronze Bell from Historic Madrasa
Description: A bronze bell used in one of the historic madrasas of Sonargaon, the ancient medieval capital of Bengal. The bell was rung to mark the times of prayer, lessons, and meals. It bears a simple engraved inscription in Arabic giving the name of the institution. Educational bells are rare survivors from pre-modern Bengal's institutional life. Sonargaon was the seat of learning and governance in medieval Bengal, and this bell is a tangible remnant of its scholarly institutions.

Artifact_Name: Alphabet Chart in Bengali Script (Bornomala)
Description: A printed Bengali alphabet chart (bornomala) produced for primary school classrooms in the early 20th century. The chart displays the full set of Bengali vowels (swar) and consonants (byanjan) with accompanying illustrations for each letter — a fish for 'mach', a bird for 'pakhi', a hand for 'hath'. The illustrations are drawn in a charming folk-art style and printed by lithography. Such charts were the first introduction to literacy for generations of Bengali children and represent the early development of educational print culture in Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Traditional Patachitra (Scroll Painting)
Description: A patachitra (narrative scroll painting) from Narsingdi, depicting the story of the demon king Ravana and Lord Rama in a sequence of illustrated panels. Made by a patua (scroll painter) using natural pigments derived from plants and minerals on handmade paper. The patua traditionally traveled from village to village unrolling the scroll while singing the story depicted. Patachitra is one of Bangladesh's oldest living art traditions, combining visual art with oral performance. The colors are vivid — red, yellow, green, and black — and the style is highly stylized with flat perspective.

Artifact_Name: Children's Game Set — Ludo and Shataranj (Chess)
Description: A set of traditional indoor games including a hand-painted ludo board and a carved wooden chess (shataranj) set. The ludo board is decorated with folk motifs in bright colors; the chess pieces are carved in the traditional South Asian style with elephant, horse, and foot-soldier pieces. These games represent the intellectual and recreational culture of Bengali children across social classes. Chess (shataranj) came to Bengal through the Mughal period and became deeply embedded in urban household culture, while ludo developed from ancient Indian games of chance.

Artifact_Name: Eid Card Collection (Historical)
Description: A framed collection of twelve historical Eid greeting cards from the 1960s and 1970s, representing the evolution of festive card design in Bangladesh. The cards combine Islamic calligraphy with Bengali folk motifs — flowers, birds, and rural scenes. Several are hand-painted by commercial artists; others are lithographs. The exchange of Eid cards became a beloved cultural practice in Bengali Muslim homes after the 1950s, blending religious celebration with artistic expression. The collection documents a vanishing tradition as digital communication has replaced paper cards.

Artifact_Name: Model of a Traditional Bengali Village (Diorama)
Description: A detailed scale model depicting a traditional Bengali village (gram): bamboo-walled thatched houses, a pond with lotus flowers, rice fields, a banyan tree, a mosque, a school, and miniature figures of villagers going about their daily activities. Made by Shishu Academy craftspeople using clay, bamboo, and painted paper. The model was created as an educational tool to help urban children understand rural life. It captures the ecological and social structure of a typical village in the Bengal delta — the homestead (bari), the courtyard (uthan), the vegetable garden (bagicha), and the community well.

Artifact_Name: First Edition of Abol Tabol by Sukumar Ray
Description: A rare first edition copy of Abol Tabol (Nonsense Rhymes) by Sukumar Ray (1887–1923), the most celebrated work of Bengali children's literature. Published in 1923, the year of Ray's death, Abol Tabol is a collection of absurdist poems illustrated by the author himself, combining wordplay, surreal imagery, and sharp social satire. The book created an entirely new genre of children's literature in Bengali and remains the most read and memorized collection of verse by Bengali children worldwide. This copy is in remarkably good condition, with the original cloth binding and all illustrations intact.

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Horse from Bisnupur Tradition
Description: A hand-modeled terracotta horse with rider, made in the tradition of the Bisnupur ceramic toys of Bengal. The horse is painted in red and white with geometric decorations. Such terracotta horses were offered at village shrines and sold at rural fairs as toys and votive objects. They are among the most ancient forms of Bengali folk art, with parallels stretching back to the Harappan civilization. The modeling is bold and simplified, capturing the essence of movement in a few expressive forms. The rider carries a sword and wears a peaked hat, possibly representing a folk hero.

Artifact_Name: Bamboo Flute (Bashi) Collection
Provenance_Note: Donated by musicians and folk artists
Description: A display of ten traditional bamboo flutes (bashi) of varying sizes, from different regions of Bangladesh. The bashi is the most iconic instrument of Bengali folk music, associated with the legendary flute-player Lord Krishna and with the baul (wandering mystic) musical tradition. Each flute is hand-crafted from a single bamboo internode, with finger holes bored by a heated iron rod. The examples here come from Sylhet and the Chittagong Hill Tracts, where distinct local playing styles have developed. Several are decorated with carved geometric patterns or wrapped with colored thread.

Artifact_Name: Photograph Archive — Children's Language Movement 1952
Provenance_Note: Donated by Press Institute of Bangladesh
Description: A collection of twelve black and white photographic prints documenting the participation of school children in the Bengali Language Movement protests of February 1952. The photographs show young students marching in Dhaka, gathering near Dhaka Medical College, and participating in memorial ceremonies. Children were among the most active participants in the Language Movement, and their courage contributed to making Bengali an official language of Pakistan in 1956. These photographs are among the most important documentary records of children's role in Bangladesh's political history.

Artifact_Name: Illustrated Story Book — Thakurmar Jhuli (Grandmother's Bag of Tales)
Description: A facsimile reproduction of the first edition of Thakurmar Jhuli (1907) by Dakshinaranjan Mitra Majumder — the most important collection of Bengali fairy tales and folk stories. The book contains stories of princes and princesses, demons (rakshas), magical birds, and enchanted forests drawn from the oral storytelling tradition of rural Bengal. The original illustrations in this edition are woodcuts in the folk style. Thakurmar Jhuli has been the primary source of magical folk narratives for Bengali children for over a century and was later made into an iconic animated film.

Artifact_Name: Hand-woven Muslin Sample (Dhakai Muslin)
Provenance_Note: Donated by master weaver family, Rupganj
Description: A framed sample of authentic Dhakai muslin — the legendary woven cotton so fine it was called 'woven air' (bafta hawa) by Mughal emperors and 'running water' (rogan pani) by European traders. This sample, woven in the 1950s by one of the last master weavers of the tradition, demonstrates the extraordinary fineness: a full sari of this fabric, 6 meters long, could be folded into a matchbox. The muslin is woven from the thread of Phuti karpas cotton grown only in a narrow strip of land along the Meghna river. The tradition was nearly destroyed by colonial policies and the advent of machine textiles.

Artifact_Name: Baul Singer's Ektara and Dotara
Description: An ektara (one-string drone lute) and a dotara (two-string melody lute) belonging to a baul singer from the Kushtia region — the heartland of the baul tradition associated with the mystic poet Lalon Shah (1774–1890). The ektara consists of a dried gourd resonator with a bamboo neck and a single metal string, played by squeezing the bamboo to change pitch. The dotara is a more complex plucked lute with two wire strings and a wooden body. These instruments are inseparable from baul philosophy, which sees music as the path to the divine. The baul tradition of Bangladesh and West Bengal was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2008.

Artifact_Name: Children's Drawing — Liberation War Series (1971)
Provenance_Note: Donated by children's war memorial project
Description: A collection of fifteen drawings made by Dhaka schoolchildren in 1972, one year after independence, depicting their memories and imaginings of the 1971 Liberation War. The drawings show Pakistani soldiers, freedom fighters (muktijoddha), burning villages, the national flag, and portraits of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman. Made with crayons and pencils, the works are raw and deeply moving documents of how children processed the trauma and triumph of the war. They were collected as part of an early Shishu Academy project to document children's responses to independence.

Artifact_Name: Brass Hookah (Huqqa) with Children's Motifs
Description: A tall brass hookah (huqqa) decorated with engraved scenes of children at play — flying kites, spinning tops, swimming in ponds, and catching fish. While hookahs were adult objects, this example is unusual in that its decorative program is entirely devoted to childhood scenes. The engraving is of the highest quality, with each scene framed in floral cartouches in the Mughal decorative tradition. The glass water vessel at the base is original, preserved intact. This object illustrates how childhood was conceptualized and depicted in late 19th-century Bengali decorative arts.

Artifact_Name: Model Boat — Traditional Fishing Vessel (Dingi)
Description: A detailed scale model of a traditional dingi fishing boat used in the rivers and coastal waters of southern Bangladesh. The model shows the flat-bottomed hull, the small covered cabin, the single mast with a cotton sail, and fishing nets coiled at the stern. River boats (nauka) are central to the culture and economy of Bangladesh, where thousands of rivers create the arterial system of a nation. The model was made by a master boatbuilder from Barisal and represents the craft knowledge of boat-building communities that has sustained life on the Bengal delta for millennia.

Artifact_Name: Hand-embroidered Schoolbag (Pothi Bag)
Description: A hand-embroidered jute schoolbag (pothi bag) made by a rural woman for her child to carry books to school. The bag is embroidered with a scene of a schoolhouse, trees, children playing, and the Bengali letters 'ba' for 'boi' (book). Made from locally grown jute cloth with cotton thread embroidery in red and green. Such bags were a labor of love, each one unique, representing the aspirations of rural families for their children's education. Jute — Bangladesh's golden fiber — forms the material base of this humble but touching artifact.

Artifact_Name: Poster — International Children's Day (1974)
Description: A original offset lithograph poster produced by Children's Museum (Shishu Academy) for International Children's Day 1974 — the second year of Bangladesh's independent existence as a nation. The poster shows a group of children of different backgrounds playing together under a rainbow, with the Bengali text 'Amader shishu, amader asha' (Our children, our hope). Designed by a prominent Dhaka graphic artist, the poster represents the early nation's aspirations for children as the foundation of the new Bangladesh. It is among the earliest graphic design artifacts in the Shishu Academy's collection.

Artifact_Name: Traditional Kite Collection (Ghuri)
Description: A collection of twelve traditional Bengali kites (ghuri) in various shapes and sizes — diamond kites, bird-shaped kites, and the large 'pataug' display kite. Made from split bamboo frames covered with colored tissue paper, decorated with cut-paper patterns. Kite-flying (ghuri ura) is one of the most beloved seasonal pastimes in Bangladesh, particularly during the winter months and at the Sakrain festival in Old Dhaka. The competitive sport of kite-fighting (ghuri kata) — cutting opponents' strings with glass-coated 'manja' thread — has been a defining feature of Dhaka's cultural life for centuries.

Artifact_Name: Certificate of the First National Children's Literature Award (1976)
Description: The original certificate awarded at the first Children's Museum (Shishu Academy) National Children's Literature Award ceremony in 1976, presented to a pioneering author of Bengali children's fiction. The certificate is hand-calligraphed in Bengali on cream parchment with gold borders and bears the official seal of Children's Museum (Shishu Academy) and the signature of the cultural minister. The establishment of a national children's literature prize in 1976 — just five years after independence — reflected the new nation's commitment to building a distinct cultural identity for its youngest citizens. The award continues to be presented annually.

Artifact_Name: Dingi Boat
Finding_Place: Collected from riverine communities of Bangladesh
Description: The Dingi is one of the most common and traditional small boats of Bangladesh, used widely across rivers and canals for everyday transport, fishing, and household use. A small, narrow, flat-bottomed rowboat typically made of wood, it is found throughout riverine Bangladesh. Explicitly named in the CholoZai source listing the museum's collection.

Artifact_Name: Ekmalai Boat
Description: The Ekmalai is a traditional Bangladeshi boat type preserved and displayed in the museum. Listed among the boat types in the museum's collection in the CholoZai source. Specific details about its use and origin region are not stated in the available sources.

Artifact_Name: Pansi Boat
Description: The Pansi is a traditional Bangladeshi sailing and rowing boat with a distinctive long, narrow hull. It is historically used for transport of goods and passengers along rivers in southern Bangladesh, including the Barisal and coastal regions. Listed among the boat types in the museum's collection.

Artifact_Name: Gayna Boat
Description: The Gayna (also Gaina) is a traditional decorated Bangladeshi boat, often associated with ceremonial or festive use. Listed among the named boat types in the museum's collection in the CholoZai source. Specific regional details not stated in available sources.

Artifact_Name: Keraya Boat
Description: The Keraya is a traditional Bangladeshi boat type included in the museum's collection. Listed by name in the CholoZai source among the variety of boats displayed. No further details are available in the cited sources.

Artifact_Name: Kosha Boat
Description: The Kosha is a traditional narrow, wooden fishing and transport boat used in Bangladesh's riverine waterways. Listed among the named boat types in the museum's collection. Also known as a dugout-style craft in some regions.

Artifact_Name: Konda Boat
Description: The Konda is a traditional Bangladeshi boat type included in the museum's collection. Listed by name in the CholoZai source. No further details available in the cited sources.

Artifact_Name: Ghasi Boat
Description: The Ghasi is a traditional Bangladeshi boat type preserved and displayed in the museum. Listed among the named boat types in the CholoZai source. Specific regional or use details are not stated in the available sources.

Artifact_Name: Sampan Boat
Finding_Place: Collected from coastal and riverine communities
Description: The Sampan is a flat-bottomed wooden boat widely used along the rivers and coastal areas of Bangladesh and Southeast Asia. It is used for fishing, transport, and daily life along waterways. Listed in the museum's collection by name in the CholoZai source (listed twice in the original source text, suggesting possibly multiple variants or regional types of Sampan were displayed).

Artifact_Name: Lambapadi Boat
Description: The Lambapadi is a traditional Bangladeshi boat type included in the museum's collection. Listed by name in the CholoZai source. 'Lamba' in Bengali means long, suggesting a long-hulled vessel design. No further details are available in the cited sources.

Artifact_Name: Kathami / Export Boat
Description: The Kathami, also called 'Export' boat, is a traditional Bangladeshi boat type included in the museum's collection. The CholoZai source lists it as 'Kathami or Export', indicating these are local names for the same vessel type. No further details are stated in the available sources.

Artifact_Name: Bachari Boat
Description: The Bachari is a traditional Bangladeshi boat type preserved and displayed in the museum. Listed among the named boat types in the CholoZai source. TripMonarch also mentions the goal of preserving 'extinct Bahari shaped boats', suggesting Bachari/Bahari may be among the extinct types documented in the museum.

Artifact_Name: Patam Boat
Description: The Patam is a traditional Bangladeshi boat type included in the museum's collection. Listed by name in the CholoZai source. No further details on its region of use or status are stated in the available sources.

Artifact_Name: Baich Boat (Racing Boat)
Description: The Baich boat is the traditional Bangladeshi racing boat, used in the famous Naukabai (boat race) festivals, which are an integral part of Bengali culture and heritage. Boat races (Naukabai) have historically been associated with Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman and Bengali cultural identity, making this a symbolically significant exhibit. Listed among the named boat types in the CholoZai source.

Artifact_Name: Bangabandhu and Liberation War Corner
Finding_Place: Established 31 December 2020 within the museum complex
Description: A dedicated section within the museum documenting the connection between Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, the Bangladesh Liberation War, and the cultural/historical significance of boats to Bangladesh. The museum was named in honor of Mujib Year (birth centenary of Bangabandhu). Explicitly mentioned in Wikipedia as a facility inside the museum complex.

Artifact_Name: Boat Research Center
Finding_Place: Established 31 December 2020 within the museum complex
Description: A research center within the museum complex dedicated to the study and documentation of traditional Bangladeshi boats. The museum aimed to preserve portraits, information, and specimens of boats from different regions of Bangladesh. Explicitly mentioned in Wikipedia as a facility of the museum.

Artifact_Name: Modern Library
Finding_Place: Established 31 December 2020 within the museum complex
Description: A modern library within the museum complex, aimed at housing books, research materials, and documentation related to Bangladesh's boat heritage and riverine history. Explicitly mentioned in Wikipedia as a facility of the museum.

Artifact_Name: Children's Recreation Center
Finding_Place: Established 31 December 2020 within the museum complex
Description: A children's recreation and entertainment center within the museum complex, aimed at making the museum accessible and engaging for younger visitors. Explicitly mentioned in Wikipedia as a facility of the museum.

Artifact_Name: Food Court
Finding_Place: Established 31 December 2020 within the museum complex
Description: A food court facility within the museum complex, designed to make the museum a self-contained visitor destination. Explicitly mentioned in Wikipedia as a facility of the museum.

Artifact_Name: Tārā
Description: A bronze image of the goddess Tārā, one of the most revered female Bodhisattvas in Vajrayana Buddhism. Tārā is the compassionate saviour deity and her form is found in multiple variants at Mainamati. This piece is part of the rich bronze collection of the museum.

Artifact_Name: Avalokiteśvara
Description: A bronze image of Avalokiteśvara (Lokeśvara), the Bodhisattva of infinite compassion — one of the most frequently depicted deities in the Mainamati bronze corpus. A colossal example was found at Ānanda Vihāra, and a large bronze head near Kutila Mura.

Artifact_Name: Manasā
Description: Manasā, the Bengali folk goddess of serpents, depicted surrounded by cobras. She is one of the most distinctive deities found in the Mainamati region, reflecting the syncretic blend of Buddhist and Hindu folk worship characteristic of early medieval southeast Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Naṭarāja (Dancing Śiva)
Description: Naṭarāja — Śiva as the Lord of Dance — depicted in his cosmic Āṇanda Tāṇḍava dance posture. This multi-armed form of Śiva symbolises the eternal cycles of creation, preservation and destruction. Found at Mainamati-Lalmai ridge, it reflects Brahmanical influence alongside Buddhist art.

Artifact_Name: Umā-Maheśvara
Description: Umā-Maheśvara — Śiva and his consort Pārvatī (Umā) depicted together seated on Mount Kailāsa in a scene of divine domestic bliss. Reflects the Brahmanical patronage coexisting with Buddhism at Mainamati.

Artifact_Name: Pārvatī (Standing)
Description: A standing image of Pārvatī, the Hindu goddess and consort of Śiva, depicted in elegant tribhaṅga posture with her characteristic attributes. Reflects the Hindu sculptural tradition that flourished alongside Buddhism in the Mainamati region.

Artifact_Name: Vajrasattva (Colossal Bronze)
Description: The magnificent colossal bronze Vajrasattva — 1.10 m high in seated position — considered one of the finest examples of bronze casting from the Indian subcontinent. Vajrasattva represents all five Tathāgatas simultaneously. Found at Bhoja Vihāra; the donor was clearly a very wealthy merchant or royal dignitary of the Candra dynasty.

Artifact_Name: Cāmuṇḍā
Description: Cāmuṇḍā, the fierce goddess and one of the Saptamātrkā (seven mother goddesses), depicted in her terrifying emaciated form dancing on a corpse. Her presence at Mainamati reflects the Tantric traditions of early medieval southeast Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Navagraha (Nine Planets Panel)
Description: A Navagraha panel depicting the nine planetary deities: Sūrya, Candra, Maṅgala, Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śani, Rāhu and Ketu. Such panels were placed above temple doorways as protective devices in the Hindu/Brahmanical tradition of medieval Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Weighing Scales & Weights (Balance & Measures)
Description: A collection of weighing instruments and standardised weights (bāṭkhārā) recovered from Mainamati excavations. These attest to active trade and commerce at Mainamati-Devaparvata. The presence of standardised weights confirms the town's role as a major riverine trade port on the banks of the Kṣirodā river.

Artifact_Name: Stucco Akṣobhya (Buddha, In Situ)
Description: The most striking discovery of Itakhola Mura Vihāra — a stucco figure of Buddha Akṣobhya preserved in situ. Stucco figures were common in Gandhāra art but rare in Bengal, making this exceptional. Akṣobhya is the 'Unshakeable' Dhyāni Buddha of the eastern direction.

Artifact_Name: Standing Buddha (Life-size, Sandstone)
Description: A life-size standing sandstone image of the Buddha discovered from a chamber of the temple at Rupban Mura Vihāra. Standing 2.15 m high, it is one of the most impressive stone sculptures from Mainamati. Rupban Mura Vihāra is considered the earliest of the excavated monasteries at Mainamati.

Artifact_Name: Colossal Bronze Buddha (Museum Entrance)
Description: A colossal seated bronze Buddha displayed to the left of the museum entrance — the first major piece visitors encounter. A key highlight of the museum's collection representing the early Tantric Buddhist artistic tradition of southeast Bengal. Dated to the 7th century CE.

Artifact_Name: Mahāpratisarā (Metal Image)
Description: Mahāpratisarā — 'the great amulet' — a multi-armed Buddhist protective goddess. This metal image from Rupban Mura is one of the important protective deity images from Mainamati. She is worshipped for warding off misfortune and danger.

Artifact_Name: Colossal Bronze Avalokiteśvara (Ānanda Vihāra)
Provenance_Note: Excavation — Ānanda Vihāra (Deva Dynasty, Śrī Ānanda Deva)
Description: A colossal bronze Avalokiteśvara recovered from Ānanda Vihāra — the largest Buddhist monastery in Mainamati (195 m a side), built by Śrī Ānanda Deva, third ruler of the Deva dynasty. One of the most important bronze sculptures from the entire Mainamati corpus.

Artifact_Name: Bronze Avalokiteśvara Head (Large, Kutila Mura)
Description: A large life-size bronze head of Avalokiteśvara collected near Kutila Mura. Its identification is based on the miniature figure of Amitābha on its exquisitely ornamented crown. Dated to around the 10th century CE — one of the most impressive bronzes from Mainamati.

Artifact_Name: Bronze Votive Stupa (with Four Female Deities)
Description: A remarkable bronze votive stupa found during excavations at Salban Vihāra, with four female deities on four sides each seated under a shrine placed against the drum of the stupa. A unique example of votive Buddhist metalwork from medieval southeast Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Sealings (Śrī Bhavadeva Mahāvihāra)
Provenance_Note: Excavation — Salban Vihāra (Deva Dynasty, Śrī Bhavadeva)
Description: Terracotta sealings bearing the inscription: 'Śrī-Bhavadeva Mahā Vihāra-Ārya-Bhikṣu-Saṃghasya' — 'of the order of the noble monks of the monastic establishment of Śrī Bhavadeva.' These confirm King Bhavadeva of the Deva dynasty as patron of Salban Vihāra.

Artifact_Name: Copper Plate Grants (Collection of Seven)
Provenance_Note: Excavation — Salban Vihāra (Khadga, Rata, Deva, Candra Dynasties)
Description: Seven copper plate inscriptions from Salban Vihāra representing multiple dynasties. Key plates: Kailan copper plate of Śrīdhāranarāta (c. 665–675 CE); copper plate of Rajputra Balabhaṭṭa (c. 715–730 CE); Asiatic Society copper plate of Bhavadeva (c. 815–840 CE); Pascimbhāgh copper plate of Śrīcandra (c. 925–975 CE). Primary sources for the history of southeast Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Gold & Silver Coins (~350 pieces)
Provenance_Note: Excavation — Multiple Sites (Khadga, Harikela-Paṭṭikera, Candra Dynasties)
Description: Approximately 350 gold and silver coins recovered from Mainamati sites, primarily from Salban Vihāra. Includes Gupta imitation gold coins, Harikela-Paṭṭikera type silver coins from Rupban Mura, and Pāṭṭikera style silver coins from Itakhola Mura. Provide crucial evidence for dating the sites and the prosperity of Mainamati as a trade centre.

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Plaques (Large Collection)
Finding_Place: Salban Vihāra / Bhoja Vihāra, Mainamati, Comilla
Description: Hundreds of terracotta plaques recovered from Salban Vihāra and Bhoja Vihāra depicting Buddhist, Hindu and secular subjects. Bhoja Vihāra's central temple was 'profusely decorated' with such plaques. They represent one of the richest terracotta collections from medieval Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Clay Votive Stupas & Seals (Kutila Mura)
Description: Innumerable tiny terracotta and clay votive stupas, seals and sealings enshrined within the eight box-chambers of the Dharmacakra-shaped foundation of the central stupa at Kutila Mura. Together with fine Buddhist sculptures in soft grey shale, these represent a unique and rare ritual deposit.

Artifact_Name: Buddhist Sculptures in Soft Grey Shale (Kutila Mura)
Description: A class of fine Buddhist sculptures in soft grey shale found within the stupa chambers of Kutila Mura. Distinguished by the use of softer grey shale rather than the black basalt typical of the Pāla period, suggesting an earlier regional tradition. Includes an Avalokiteśvara seated on a principal lotus with attendants.

Artifact_Name: Copper Plate Inscription (Itakhola Mura)
Description: A copper plate inscription recovered from Itakhola Mura Vihāra — one of the two earliest monasteries at Mainamati, built by Khadga King Balabhaṭṭa. An important epigraphic record for the early history of southeast Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Bronze Votive Images — Amitābha, Akṣobhya & Gaṇeśa
Description: Six bronze votive images recovered from Itakhola Mura Vihāra: images of Amitābha, Akṣobhya and Gaṇeśa. The Buddhist images bear a stamped Buddhist creed on their back — a distinctive feature. Gaṇeśa's presence alongside Buddhist deities reflects religious syncretism at Mainamati.

Artifact_Name: Amitābha (Bhoja Vihāra, Medium Bronze)
Description: A medium-size soft-shell image of Amitābha, the 'Infinite Light' Dhyāni Buddha of the western direction, found at Bhoja Vihāra. Amitābha was among the most popular Dhyāni Buddhas in medieval Bangladesh, depicted in dhyāna mudrā (meditation posture).

Artifact_Name: Akṣobhya (Bhoja Vihāra, Medium Bronze)
Description: A medium-size soft-shell image of Akṣobhya ('the Imperturbable'), the blue Dhyāni Buddha of the eastern direction, found at Bhoja Vihāra. Along with Amitābha, Akṣobhya was one of the most popular Dhyāni Buddhas at Mainamati.

Artifact_Name: Harikela-Paṭṭikera Silver Coins
Finding_Place: Bhoja Vihāra / Rupban Mura, Mainamati, Comilla
Description: Harikela-Paṭṭikera type silver coins found at multiple Mainamati sites including Bhoja Vihāra and Rupban Mura. Pāṭṭikera (modern Paitkara, Comilla) was an important administrative seat that eventually formed a separate kingdom with ties to Pagan (Bagan) and Arakan of Myanmar.

Artifact_Name: Large Bronze Bell
Description: A massive bronze bell weighing 370 kg — one of the museum's most dramatic exhibits. Bronze bells were used in Buddhist religious ceremonies. The museum also holds a separate giant bronze object weighing approximately 500 kg. These bells attest to the sophisticated metal-casting technology of medieval Mainamati.

Artifact_Name: Nandī (Śiva's Bull, Black Stone)
Description: A black stone sculpture of Nandī, the sacred bull and vehicle (vāhana) of Lord Śiva. This Brahmanical sculpture is one of several Hindu pieces in the Mainamati collection, reflecting the multi-religious nature of medieval southeast Bengal where Charpatra Mura was the only purely Brahmanical site.

Artifact_Name: Burmese Manuscript on Palm Leaves
Description: An ancient manuscript written on palm leaves in the Burmese script, attesting to the cultural and religious connections between Mainamati-Pāṭṭikera and Myanmar (Pagan and Arakan). Reflects the wider cultural network through which the art idiom of Mainamati spread to Myanmar and Java.

Artifact_Name: Iron Objects & Tools
Description: A collection of iron objects — tools and implements — recovered from Mainamati excavations, demonstrating the iron-working technology of medieval inhabitants. Iron objects include agricultural and craft tools that sustained the economic activities supporting the monasteries.

Artifact_Name: Clay Toys (Various)
Description: A variety of clay toys — animals, figurines and objects — recovered from Mainamati excavations. These secular objects provide evidence of daily life and material culture of the lay population that supported the Buddhist monastic complex at Mainamati-Devaparvata.

Artifact_Name: Pottery Collection (Various Types)
Description: A large pottery collection including Common Light Gray Ware recovered from the Mainamati excavations. Changes in pottery type help archaeologists distinguish the two major historic phases of Mainamati (6th–13th century CE). Increase in Common Light Gray Ware marks the second historic phase associated with the Candra dynasty.

Artifact_Name: Miniature Bronze Buddha Images (Collection)
Description: Over 150 miniature bronze Buddha images recovered mostly from the monastic cells and votive deposits at Mainamati — the largest such collection from medieval Bengal. These were used for personal devotion and as votive offerings. They represent the Tantric Buddhist pantheon: Dhyāni Buddhas, Bodhisattvas and Tārās.

Artifact_Name: Semi-precious Stone Beads
Description: A collection of semi-precious stone beads including carnelian and agate recovered from Ānanda Vihāra and other Mainamati sites. These beads attest to trade contacts and the material wealth of the monastery patrons, reflecting long-distance trade networks linking Mainamati to wider South and Southeast Asia.

Artifact_Name: Padmapāṇi / Bodhisattva (Standing Bronze, Salban Vihāra)
Description: A standing bronze Bodhisattva Padmapāṇi ('lotus-bearer'), a form of Avalokiteśvara holding a lotus. One of the many bronzes recovered from Salban Vihāra's 115 monastic cells and surrounding excavations. It is identified in the museum as 'Bodhisattva Padmapāṇi, Salban Vihāra.'

Artifact_Name: Lokottara Buddha Statues (Stone, Multiple)
Description: Various types of standing Lokottara ('supramundane') Buddha statues in stone. Lokottara Buddha images represent the transcendent aspect of the Buddha beyond his human manifestation — a key concept in Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna Buddhism. Multiple examples are on display in the museum.

Artifact_Name: Trivikrama Viṣṇu (Stone)
Description: A stone image of Viṣṇu in his Trivikrama form — the three-strides dwarf avatāra (Vāmana) — depicting his cosmic stride that covered earth, sky and heaven. This Vaiṣṇava sculptural subject reflects the Hindu traditions coexisting with Buddhism at Mainamati during the Candra period.

Artifact_Name: Mahiṣamardinī Durgā (Stone)
Description: A stone image of Durgā slaying the buffalo demon Mahiṣāsura — the most iconic form of the goddess Durgā in Hindu iconography. Reflects the multi-religious character of Mainamati where Buddhist and Hindu (Śākta) traditions coexisted during the Candra period.

Artifact_Name: Mārīcī (Stone)
Description: A stone image of Mārīcī, the Buddhist goddess of dawn and light, depicted with multiple arms. Mārīcī was a popular goddess in Tantric Buddhism of medieval Bengal. Images of this goddess are found at both Mainamati and other major Buddhist sites of Bangladesh.

Artifact_Name: Mañjuśrī (Stone)
Description: A stone image of Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva of wisdom, holding his characteristic sword (to cut through ignorance) and the Prajñāpāramitā text. The seated form of this deity is also known as Mañjuvara. Mañjuśrī was one of the key Bodhisattvas worshipped at Mainamati.

Artifact_Name: Woodwork Patterns / Wooden Artifacts
Description: Preserved woodwork patterns and wooden artifacts recovered from Mainamati excavations. Given the humid delta climate of Bengal, wooden objects rarely survive in the archaeological record, making these fragments particularly rare and valuable.

Artifact_Name: Gupta Imitation Gold Coins (5 pieces)
Description: Five Gupta imitation gold coins recovered from Rupban Mura Vihāra — among the earliest datable objects from Mainamati. These coins suggest the site's origins in the late Gupta or immediately post-Gupta period (6th–7th century CE) and confirm the first historic phase of Mainamati.

Artifact_Name: Pāṭṭikera Style Silver Coin (Itakhola Mura)
Description: A Pāṭṭikera style silver coin salvaged from Itakhola Mura Vihāra. The name Pāṭṭikera appears in coin legends from the 8th century CE levels of Salban Vihāra and also in the Cambridge University Manuscript of Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā (copied in 1015 CE). Pāṭṭikera eventually formed a separate kingdom.

Artifact_Name: Nagraja
Finding_Place: Nārāyanpur, Barurā Police Station, Comilla District
Provenance_Note: Collection — Nārāyanpur, Barurā, Comilla (Dept. of Archaeology, Bangladesh)
Description: Nārāyanpur, Barurā Police Station, Comilla District

Artifact_Name: Snake and Mongoose Terracotta Plaque
Description: A terracotta relief plaque from Salban Vihāra depicting a snake and mongoose in combat — a motif of profound symbolic significance in South Asian iconography. The snake–mongoose combat symbolises the eternal conflict between earth and the underworld, life and death, and is a common auspicious subject on Buddhist and Hindu decorative plaques. This piece is part of the rich terracotta assemblage recovered from Salban Vihāra's central temple, which was 'profusely decorated' with such plaques. The terracotta modelling is characteristically bold and vigorous, typical of 8th century CE Samatata workmanship. Source: ResearchGate, Double-bodied lion and related Salban Vihāra terracotta series (fig. 307670905); Dept. of Archaeology, Bangladesh.

Artifact_Name: Double-Bodied Lion (Vyāla / Śārdūla)
Description: A remarkable architectural sculpture of a double-bodied lion (dvimukha vyāla or śārdūla) — a single leonine head with two bodies extending in opposite directions — carved from buff sandstone at Salban Vihāra. Such double-bodied mythical creatures served as decorative and apotropaic (protective) elements on Buddhist temple architecture, typically placed at corners of temple bases or friezes. The image demonstrates the sophisticated stone-carving tradition at Mainamati alongside its more celebrated bronze corpus. The motif of the vyāla — a rearing composite leonine beast — is widespread in South Asian temple architecture from the Gupta period onwards. Source: ResearchGate fig. 307670905; 'Double-bodied lion, 8th Century CE, Salabana Vihara, Mainamati Museum, Bangladesh.'

Artifact_Name: Stone Sculptures Display (Four Deities Pane
Description: A display group of four important stone deity sculptures mounted in the main gallery against a magenta-red velvet backing (image: mainamati3.webp). From left to right: (1) a multi-armed standing deity with attendants — possibly Viṣṇu or a Bodhisattva, found likely at Mainamati-Lalmai; (2) a standing deity with globe and serpent attributes, from Gujrābar, Artisha, Comilla (per museum label, 8th–10th century CE); (3) a multi-armed standing deity with rich jewellery and attendant figures, also from Gujrābar, Artisha, Comilla; (4) a dancing deity figure — possibly Naṭarāja or Heruka. The museum label for the second figure reads 'Gujrābar, Artisha, Comilla' and dates it to the Pāla period. This display showcases the full range of Buddhist and Brahmanical sculptural production from the greater Comilla-Samatata region. Source: Museum display photograph; Dept. of Archaeology, Bangladesh.

Artifact_Name: Cyclostyle Duplicating Machine
Description: A stencil duplicating machine used by Bangabandhu after 7 March 1971 to send messages to party leaders, newspapers, and the people of Bangladesh during the non-cooperation movement.

Artifact_Name: Telephone Set (Independence Declaration)
Description: The telephone set located on the south side of the personal library, near the door. Bangabandhu used this phone to announce the freedom of the Bengali nation; the declaration was transmitted via wireless, telephone and telegram across Bangladesh.

Artifact_Name: Bullet-Pierced Books (Library Collection)
Description: A collection of books of famous writers and novelists kept by Bangabandhu in his personal library. The books bear visible bullet holes from the attack on the house during the night of 25 March 1971, serving as physical evidence of the violence.

Artifact_Name: Portrait Gallery of Assassinated Family Members
Description: Framed portraits displayed on the eastern and western walls of the ground-floor corridor depicting the deceased family members of Bangabandhu along with guests who were killed in the house on 15 August 1975.

Artifact_Name: Dressing Table (Bangabandhu's Bedroom)
Description: The original dressing table from Bangabandhu and Begum Mujib's bedroom on the second floor. The furniture still displays blood-spots and bullet marks from the assassination of 15 August 1975.

Artifact_Name: Desk Table (Bangabandhu's Bedroom)
Description: Original desk table from Bangabandhu's bedroom on the second floor, bearing bullet marks and blood-spots from the assassination of 15 August 1975.

Artifact_Name: Reading Table (Bangabandhu's Bedroom)
Description: Original reading table from Bangabandhu's bedroom, displaying physical evidence of the 15 August 1975 assassination through bullet marks and blood-spots.

Artifact_Name: Betel Vase (Bangabandhu's Bedroom)
Description: A betel (paan) vase that was part of the personal effects in Bangabandhu's bedroom. Preserved as a personal relic bearing blood-spots and bullet damage from the 1975 assassination.

Artifact_Name: Letter to Bangamata
Description: A preserved letter addressed to Bangamata (Sheikh Fazilatunnesa Mujib), kept in Bangabandhu's bedroom on the second floor. One of the personal documents recovered after the family regained the house.

Artifact_Name: Dining Table
Description: The original dining table placed near the entrance of the family dining room on the first floor. Bangabandhu and his family members used it for meals. Bangamata served food to Bangabandhu and guests at this table.

Artifact_Name: Jugs (Dining Set)
Description: Original dining jugs used by Bangabandhu and family members at the dining table in the family meeting room. Part of the preserved dining accessories.

Artifact_Name: Glasses (Dining Set)
Description: Original drinking glasses from Bangabandhu's family dining set, displayed in the family meeting room on the second floor.

Artifact_Name: Plates (Dining Set)
Description: Original dining plates from Bangabandhu's household used at family meals, now displayed on the dining table in the family meeting room.

Artifact_Name: Teacups (Dining Set)
Description: Original teacups from Bangabandhu's household, part of the preserved dining accessories displayed in the family meeting and dining room on the second floor.

Artifact_Name: Spoons (Dining Set)
Description: Original spoons from Bangabandhu's family dining set, displayed among the regular dining accessories in the family meeting room.

Artifact_Name: Knives (Dining Set)
Description: Original cutlery knives from Bangabandhu's family dining set, displayed alongside other regular dining accessories in the family meeting room.

Artifact_Name: Begum Mujib's Handmade Pickle Jar
Description: A handmade pickle jar belonging to Bangamata Sheikh Fazilatunnesa Mujib, displayed in the family dining and meeting room on the second floor as a personal relic of Bangabandhu's wife.

Artifact_Name: Sheikh Russell's Bicycle (No. 1)
Description: One of Sheikh Russell's two favourite bicycles (youngest son of Bangabandhu, born 18 October 1964, killed 15 August 1975), displayed in the family dining and meeting room.

Artifact_Name: Sheikh Russell's Bicycle (No. 2)
Description: The second of Sheikh Russell's two favourite bicycles displayed in the family dining and meeting room, a personal relic of Bangabandhu's youngest son.

Artifact_Name: Coke Bottle
Description: An original Coca-Cola bottle displayed in the family dining and meeting room, one of the personal items preserved from Bangabandhu's household.

Artifact_Name: Tin Containing Raw Rice
Description: A tin container with raw rice, preserved as a household item from Bangabandhu's family kitchen and dining area, displayed in the family meeting room.

Artifact_Name: Television Set – Citizen Brand
Description: An old Citizen brand television with a dark body, standing in the southeast corner of the family meeting room on the second floor. Bangabandhu used to sit here and watch TV with family members. Bullet marks are visible in the room.

Artifact_Name: Sheikh Russell's Ball
Description: A ball belonging to Sheikh Russell (youngest son of Bangabandhu), one of his childhood playing items preserved and displayed in the museum.

Artifact_Name: Sheikh Russell's Hockey Stick
Description: A hockey stick used by Sheikh Russell, preserved as a childhood relic of Bangabandhu's youngest son, displayed in the museum.

Artifact_Name: Sheikh Russell's Cricket Bat
Description: A cricket bat belonging to Sheikh Russell, one of his sporting items preserved and displayed in the museum.

Artifact_Name: Sheikh Russell's Helmet
Description: A helmet belonging to Sheikh Russell, preserved and displayed in the museum as part of his personal belongings.

Artifact_Name: Sheikh Russell's Aquarium
Description: An aquarium belonging to Sheikh Russell, one of the possessions of Bangabandhu's youngest son preserved and displayed in the museum.

Artifact_Name: Sheikh Russell's Toys
Description: Various childhood toys belonging to Sheikh Russell, preserved and displayed in the museum along with his other possessions.

Artifact_Name: Sheikh Russell's Watches
Description: Watches belonging to Sheikh Russell, preserved and displayed in the museum as part of his personal effects.

Artifact_Name: Tobacco Pipe of Bangabandhu
Description: Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's iconic tobacco pipe, one of his most recognized personal accessories. Originally displayed in the museum; later handed over to the Bangladesh National Museum by the Bangabandhu Memorial Trust in August 2022 with PM Sheikh Hasina's approval.

Artifact_Name: Mujib Coat (Iconic Black Coat)
Description: The iconic black sleeveless jacket (Mujib coat) worn by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, which became a symbol of his identity and the Bangladeshi independence movement. Transferred to the Bangladesh National Museum by the Bangabandhu Memorial Trust in August 2022.

Artifact_Name: White Punjabi of Bangabandhu
Description: Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's white punjabi (long shirt), part of his signature attire. Transferred to the Bangladesh National Museum by the Bangabandhu Memorial Trust in August 2022.

Artifact_Name: Pajama of Bangabandhu
Description: Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's pajama (lower garment), part of his traditional attire. Transferred to the Bangladesh National Museum by the Bangabandhu Memorial Trust in August 2022.

Artifact_Name: Eyeglasses of Bangabandhu
Description: Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's personal eyeglasses, one of his recognizable accessories, preserved and displayed in the museum along with other personal effects.

Artifact_Name: Personal Accessories of Bangabandhu (Miscellaneous)
Description: Various personal accessories and items used by Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, displayed alongside his eyeglasses and pipe as personal relics in the museum.

Artifact_Name: Diaries of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman
Description: Personal diaries found by Sheikh Hasina after the house was returned to the family in June 1981. The diaries were later edited and published as memoirs (Unfinished Memoirs / Karagarer Rojnamcha). The original manuscripts were preserved at the museum.

Artifact_Name: Bloodied Clothing (August 15 Assassination Evidence)
Description: Clothing items bearing bloodstains from the assassination of 15 August 1975, exhibited as evidence of the tragic event. The museum maintained these as part of its exhibits on the assassination.

Artifact_Name: Photographs – Bangabandhu's Life (Large Collection)
Finding_Place: Various archives, government records, personal family collection
Description: A large and rare photographic collection documenting the entire life of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, from his early political days through his role as founding president of Bangladesh. Displayed throughout the museum including the corridor gallery and ground floor.

Artifact_Name: Post-Assassination Violence Photographs
Description: Photographs documenting the aftermath of the 15 August 1975 assassination, showing the violence and destruction in the house. Displayed to remind visitors of the brutal killing.

Artifact_Name: Bullet Holes in Walls and Staircase
Description: Physical marks of bullet holes preserved in the walls of the office room, the main staircase, the bedroom, and the library of the Bangabandhu Bhaban. These serve as primary physical evidence of the 1975 assassination and cannot be separated from the building structure.

Artifact_Name: Sheikh Kamal's Room Contents / Office Room Display
Description: The ground floor office room (reception hall) where Sheikh Kamal (Bangabandhu's eldest son) was killed on 15 August 1975. The room was closed to visitors but preserves the physical evidence of the assassination including bullet marks on walls.

Artifact_Name: Sheikh Russel's Birthplace Room (Preserved)
Description: The northeast ground-floor room where Sheikh Russel was born on 18 October 1964, and originally resided by Sheikh Hasina and Sheikh Rehana. Preserved as a memorial space.

Artifact_Name: Drawing Room / Salon Furniture and Décor
Description: The furniture and interior décor of the ground-floor meeting room (salon) used by Bangabandhu for political discussions, meeting party leaders, professionals, and the public. The room was the nerve center of major political decisions from 1962 to 1971.

Artifact_Name: Gallery of Bangabandhu's Golden History (Portraits)
Description: A curated gallery of portraits and images documenting the golden history of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, displayed in the drawing room on the ground floor as visitors first enter the museum.

Artifact_Name: Sheikh Hasina's Bedroom (Preserved Room)
Description: The northeast first-floor room where Sheikh Hasina (eldest daughter of Bangabandhu) lived from 1966. The room was damaged by bullets during the 15 August 1975 assassination and was kept locked and not opened to visitors.

Artifact_Name: Main Staircase (Assassination Site of Bangabandhu)
Description: The main staircase of the Bangabandhu Bhaban where Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was killed on 15 August 1975. He descended the stairs to confront the intruding assassins and was shot on the staircase. The staircase is preserved as the primary site of the assassination.

Artifact_Name: Documents Chronicling Political Life of Bangabandhu
Description: A collection of documents, official papers, and historical records related to Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's political life, his role in the liberation war, and post-independence governance, displayed in the museum.

Artifact_Name: Newspaper and Media Reports Collection
Description: A collection of newspaper clippings and media reports covering the key political milestones of Bangabandhu's life and the Bangladesh liberation movement, incorporated into the museum's exhibits.

Artifact_Name: Sheikh Russel's Photo with Sultana Kamal
Description: A photograph of Sheikh Russell with Sultana Kamal (wife of Sheikh Kamal), preserved and displayed among Sheikh Russell's memorabilia in the museum.

Artifact_Name: Audio Recording – 7th March 1971 Speech (Archive)
Description: Audio recordings of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's historic speech of 7 March 1971 at the Suhrawardy Udyan (then Race Course Ground), recognized by UNESCO as part of the Memory of the World Register. Archived and played in the museum's auditorium/library.

Artifact_Name: Silver Filigree Model of Ahsan Manzil (pre-1888)
Finding_Place: Ahsan Manzil palace; collected by Bangladesh National Museum 1970
Description: A silver filigree model of Ahsan Manzil depicting the palace as it existed before the devastating tornado of 7 April 1888. Collected by Bangladesh National Museum in 1970 from Ahsan Manzil palace. One of two filigree models collected; this one is displayed in the museum (the other remains in Bangladesh National Museum collection). Explicitly described in the official history PDF: 'A silver filigree model of Ahsan Manzil with the feature existed before the tornado of 1888 A.D. has also been displayed here.'

Artifact_Name: Nawab-era Crockery in Original Almirahs
Finding_Place: Ahsan Manzil palace / Nawab Estate Edward House
Description: Crockery items used by the Nawabs, displayed in their original almirahs (wooden cabinets). The official history PDF states: 'Some crockery used by the Nawabs are shown in the original almirahs.' These are among the objects collected from Ahsan Manzil and Edward House.

Artifact_Name: Photographs – Dilapidated and Reconstructed Condition of Palace
Description: Photographs depicting the dilapidated state of Ahsan Manzil before restoration and its reconstructed condition after. Displayed alongside a large painting in Gallery 1. Stated in the official PDF: 'Some photographs and a big painting depict dilapidated and reconstructed condition of the palace.'

Artifact_Name: Large Painting – Dilapidated and Reconstructed Palace
Description: A large painting depicting the dilapidated and reconstructed condition of Ahsan Manzil, displayed in Gallery 1. Mentioned in the official PDF alongside photographs: 'Some photographs and a big painting depict dilapidated and reconstructed condition of the palace.'

Artifact_Name: Chandelier Shades Made of Cut Glass
Finding_Place: Ahsan Manzil palace / Nawab Estate Edward House
Description: Beautiful specimens of chandelier shades made of cut glass, displayed in Gallery 2. Explicitly named in the official PDF: 'Some beautiful specimens of chandeliers shade made of cut glass and various utensils are also displayed here.'

Artifact_Name: Various Utensils (Gallery 2 Display)
Finding_Place: Ahsan Manzil palace / Nawab Estate Edward House
Description: Various utensils of the Nawab era displayed in Gallery 2, alongside chandelier shades. The official PDF states: 'Some beautiful specimens of chandeliers shade made of cut glass and various utensils are also displayed here.'

Artifact_Name: Architectural Ground Plans (Department of Architecture)
Description: Ground plans of Ahsan Manzil made by the Department of Architecture during the palace's reconstruction, displayed in Gallery 2. The official PDF states: 'Some ground plan made by the Department of Architecture at the time of its reconstruction are also put here.'

Artifact_Name: Dining Room Almirahs (Large Wooden Cabinets)
Description: Large original almirahs (wooden cabinets) in the formal dining room of the Nawabs. The official PDF explicitly states: 'Except the candle stands, all the big almirals, mirrors and utensils made of glass and porcelain are original and were used by the Nawabs.'

Artifact_Name: Large Mirrors (Dining Room)
Description: Large original mirrors in the palace formal dining room, used by the Nawabs. The official PDF states these are original items: 'all the big almirals, mirrors and utensils made of glass and porcelain are original and were used by the Nawabs.'

Artifact_Name: Glass and Porcelain Utensils (Dining Room)
Description: Original glass and porcelain utensils used by the Nawabs in the formal dining room. The official PDF explicitly confirms these are original: 'all the big almirals, mirrors and utensils made of glass and porcelain are original and were used by the Nawabs.' Also confirmed by huntingworldbeauty (provided link): 'glass and porcelain dishes'.

Artifact_Name: Nawab Family Photographs (Dining Room Wall)
Period_Dating: Collected from Edward House during restoration 1987
Description: Photographs of the Nawab family and their guests hung on the walls of the formal dining room. The official PDF states: 'The photographs hanged on walls are from the album of the Nawabs, collected from the Edward House.'

Artifact_Name: Ceiling Fans (DC converted to AC)
Description: Original ceiling fans from the Nawab era that have been converted from DC to AC electrical system for continued use. The official PDF states: 'The ceiling fans are converted to Ac from Dc. system.' They retain their original form.

Artifact_Name: Candle Stands (Dining Room)
Finding_Place: Not confirmed as original in source
Description: Candle stands displayed in the dining room. The official PDF distinguishes these from other items: 'Except the candle stands, all the big almirals, mirrors and utensils made of glass and porcelain are original' — implying the candle stands may be replicas or newly acquired, but they are explicitly listed as part of the display.

Artifact_Name: Shield(s) – Round Room Ground Floor
Description: Shields originally belonging to the Nawabs, displayed in the Round Room on the ground floor beneath the dome. The official PDF explicitly states: 'Except the marble round table all the exhibits of the gallery are original and were used by the Nawabs. Those are shield, swords, elephant skull with tusk, buffalo head with horns and wooden partition with perforated decoration.'

Artifact_Name: Swords – Round Room Ground Floor
Description: Swords originally belonging to the Nawabs, displayed in the Round Room. The official PDF explicitly lists these as original: 'Those are shield, swords, elephant skull with tusk, buffalo head with horns and wooden partition with perforated decoration.' Also confirmed by huntingworldbeauty (provided link): 'shields, and swords'.

Artifact_Name: Elephant Skull with Tusk
Description: An elephant skull with tusk, an original exhibit in the Round Room. The official PDF explicitly lists this: 'Those are shield, swords, elephant skull with tusk, buffalo head with horns and wooden partition with perforated decoration.' Also confirmed by huntingworldbeauty (provided link): 'elephant head skeletons'.

Artifact_Name: Buffalo Head with Horns
Description: A buffalo head with horns, an original exhibit in the Round Room. The official PDF explicitly lists this: 'Those are shield, swords, elephant skull with tusk, buffalo head with horns and wooden partition with perforated decoration.'

Artifact_Name: Wooden Partition with Perforated Decoration
Description: A wooden partition featuring perforated decorative work, an original exhibit in the Round Room. Explicitly listed in the official PDF as one of the original items used by the Nawabs: 'wooden partition with perforated decoration.'

Artifact_Name: Marble Round Table – Round Room Ground Floor
Description: A marble round table in the Round Room on the ground floor. The official PDF specifically distinguishes this from the other original exhibits: 'Except the marble round table all the exhibits of the gallery are original' — indicating this table may be a replica or replacement, but it is part of the room's display.

Artifact_Name: Grand Wooden Staircase (Reconstructed)
Description: An extraordinary wooden staircase, formerly broken in parts, reconstructed according to Fritz Kapp's photograph of 1904. Its railing balusters feature cluster of grape motif decoration. The official PDF states: 'Here is an extraordinary wooden stair-case formerly broken in parts, but reconstructed according to the photograph of Fritz Kapp taken in 1904. The mind-blowing decoration used in its railing balusters is the cluster of grape motif.'

Artifact_Name: Swords – Grand Staircase
Period_Dating: Found in Ahsan Manzil; collected during restoration
Description: Swords found in Ahsan Manzil and displayed at the Grand Staircase gallery on the ground floor. The official PDF states: 'The swords, shields and spears exhibited here were found in the Ahsan Manzil.'
