Artifact_Name: 22 Listed Items from Nawab Estate Edward House (Batch Purchase 1987)
Finding_Place: Nawab Estate Office, Edward House, Dhaka
Description: A batch of 22 listed items collected from the Nawab Estate Office at Edward House through purchase in 1987. These were valuable articles shifted from Ahsan Manzil to Edward House when the palace fell into dilapidated condition in the 1970s. The official PDF states: 'In 1987 the Museum authorities collected 22 listed items from that lot through purchase.' These items are distributed across the museum galleries. Individual items within this batch that are specifically named in the PDF are catalogued in their respective gallery entries above.

Artifact_Name: Sound Dish (Sound Reflection Exhibit)
Description: Demonstrates reflection of sound and how radio receivers (radio yantra) work. Shows how sound waves behave similarly to radio waves in reception.

Artifact_Name: Magic Vision (Newton's Gravity & Relativity Monitors)
Description: Contains two monitors displaying documentary films on Newton's universal law of gravitation and Einstein's Theory of Relativity.

Artifact_Name: Touch the Fruit (Concave Mirror Focus Exhibit)
Description: Demonstrates that an object placed at the principal focus of a concave mirror creates a real image that appears wherever the mirror faces — regardless of where the mirror is positioned.

Artifact_Name: Display Phone (Video Phone Exhibit)
Description: Two display screens through which visitors can view images and talk to each other, demonstrating video telephony technology.

Artifact_Name: Magic Kettle (Continuous Boiling Water Illusion)
Description: Designed to develop visitors' thinking ability, this exhibit shows a scene of water continuously pouring from a kettle using an optical/hydraulic trick.

Artifact_Name: Balance Testing (Ear Balance Organ)
Description: The human balance organ is the ear. This exhibit demonstrates how long a person can maintain their balance with the help of their ears.

Artifact_Name: Flight Simulator
Description: A modern flight simulator using three combined displays. Visitors can experience piloting an aircraft through this interactive game.

Artifact_Name: Laser Show
Description: A short-duration video created with laser beams for the entertainment of visitors.

Artifact_Name: Spacesuit (Photo Booth)
Description: Visitors can take a photo here and the image is placed on the face of a spacesuit-clad figure displayed on the exhibit, allowing them to imagine themselves as an astronomer in a spacesuit.

Artifact_Name: Astroculture (Space Farming Model)
Description: A model of agricultural research being conducted in outer space or on a space station.

Artifact_Name: Space Agency (NASA, ESA, JAXA Linked Apple Computers)
Description: Three Apple computers linked to international space agencies — NASA, ESA, and JAXA — through which visitors can access updated research information from those institutions.

Artifact_Name: Refracting & Reflecting Telescope Models
Description: Models of both reflecting and refracting telescopes through which visitors can understand the internal structure of telescopes.

Artifact_Name: Space Sickness Exhibit
Description: A sample demonstration of the type of sickness a human experiences in outer space due to the absence of gravity.

Artifact_Name: Hand-Eye Co-ordination Exhibit
Description: Demonstrates that the hand and eye are often not well co-ordinated in many tasks, showing the frequent mismatch between hand movement and visual perception.

Artifact_Name: Mission Control (Remote Astronaut Control)
Description: Shows how an astronaut in space is controlled or monitored from Earth through mission control systems.

Artifact_Name: Moon Phases Exhibit
Description: A visitor can easily observe how the phases of the moon are created by the different relative positions of the Moon, Sun, and Earth.

Artifact_Name: VR Simulator Game
Description: A modern 360° VR simulator game that enhances cognitive thinking ability of visitors.

Artifact_Name: Plasma Tube
Description: A beam of light is visible through a gas inside a clear glass tube. The path of the light ray can be controlled by touching the tube with one's hand.

Artifact_Name: Anti-Gravity Globe
Description: A globe floating in the air that continuously rotates.

Artifact_Name: Whirlpool (Cyclone Vortex)
Description: Shows the type of vortex created in the water of a river or ocean during a cyclone.

Artifact_Name: Telescope (16-inch Newtonian Reflector)
Description: A 16-inch diameter Newtonian reflector telescope that was used in the museum's observatory until 1995.

Artifact_Name: Arch Bridge Model
Description: A bridge made of many small pieces that demonstrates why the middle section of most bridges in Bangladesh is higher (arch structure).

Artifact_Name: Gravity Well (Kepler's Laws Model)
Description: Shows actual proof of Kepler's laws related to the orbits of planets around a star.

Artifact_Name: Moon Map (Large-scale)
Description: A large-format map of the Moon.

Artifact_Name: Anousheh Ansari Memorabilia
Description: An autographed photograph of Anousheh Ansari, the first female space tourist, along with two cortpins (pins) and a badge.

Artifact_Name: Paramecium (Model)
Description: Paramecium is a unicellular organism and a member of the Paramecium genus; naturally a protozoan. Their body is tubular. The ventral and dorsal surfaces are very flat and smooth. Cytoplasmic streaming (cyclosis) can be seen in the cytoplasm of Paramecium. It feeds on bacteria, yeast cells, algae (algae) and other very tiny organisms.

Artifact_Name: Tree Fossil
Description: A fossil of a tree — petrified wood preserved as stone — displayed to illustrate geological and biological history.

Artifact_Name: Bony Fish Structure (Model)
Description: Osteichthyes (bony fish) include both marine and freshwater fish. Various changes can be seen in the classification of bony fish. Bony fish are divided into two main sub-classes: fleshy-finned fish (Sarcopterygii) and ray-finned fish (Actinopterygii).

Artifact_Name: Blue Whale Skeleton
Provenance_Note: Courtesy of Ministry of Forest & Environment
Description: A real 40-foot blue whale skeleton collected and placed in the gallery courtesy of the Ministry of Forests and Environment. It was found in the Bay of Bengal during the devastating flood of 1988.

Artifact_Name: Bacterial Cell Structure (Model)
Description: Bacteria cells generally show one or three shapes: spherical, rod, or curved-rod. If a rod is sufficiently elongated it becomes thread-like. Many bacteria have cup-shaped cell walls and are roughly oval. This cup-shaped bacterial organism is called Bacillus.

Artifact_Name: Ovarian Tumour (Specimen)
Description: A large ovarian tumour specimen weighing approximately 35 kg, collected from a hospital and preserved for display.

Artifact_Name: Amoeba (Model — Binary Fission)
Description: Amoeba is a unicellular microscopic organism. It constantly changes its shape. Amoeba is found in mud or muddy protein-free water, ponds and at the bottom of lakes. The average length of this unicellular organism is about 25 millimetres.

Artifact_Name: Liver Fluke (Model)
Description: Liver fluke is a type of internal parasite. Its shape is leaf-like and flat. It is found in the liver and gall bladder of humans. It damages the liver and causes a type of disease.

Artifact_Name: Hydra (Model)
Description: Hydra belongs to the phylum Cnidaria and the class Hydrozoa. It lives in both marine and freshwater. It has several tentacles. Its body is tubular and soft — about 10–30 mm long and 1 mm wide.

Artifact_Name: Blood Circulation System (Model)
Description: The blood circulatory system is composed of blood, blood vessels and the heart. The heart pumps blood through the vessel system with the help of cardiac muscle.

Artifact_Name: Human Brain (Model)
Description: The brain is the computer of the human body. It is divided into three parts: fore-brain (memory, hearing, vision, temperature and intelligence), mid-brain (hearing and vision) and hind-brain (body balance, blood pressure, breathing).

Artifact_Name: Human Heart (Model)
Description: The human heart is about 13 cm long and 6 cm wide. It weighs about 330 grams and is pinkish in colour but red when full of blood. The human heart has 4 chambers: upper right atrium, upper left atrium, lower right ventricle and lower left ventricle.

Artifact_Name: RNA / Ribonucleic Acid (Model)
Description: RNA is essentially a fine single strand. Single-stranded RNA carries the genetic characteristics of various viruses. It is a type of chemical compound. With the help of ribosomes, RNA synthesises proteins from DNA.

Artifact_Name: DNA / Deoxyribonucleic Acid (Model)
Description: DNA is a type of nucleic acid and a vital chemical substance of living things. DNA carries genetic characteristics. It comes from chromosomes and controls all cellular activities.

Artifact_Name: Cell Division — Meiosis (Model)
Description: Meiosis is a nuclear division skill where the number of chromosomes present in the mother nucleus is halved in each daughter nucleus. The stages are: Leptotene, Zygotene, Diplotene, Diakinesis, Metaphase-1, Anaphase-1, Telophase-1, Prophase-2, and Telophase-2.

Artifact_Name: Cell Division — Mitosis (Model)
Description: Mitosis is a nucleus division method in eukaryotic unicellular organisms and multicellular eukaryotic reproduction through cell division. Stages: Interphase, Prophase, Mid-prophase, Late anaphase, Early telophase and Late telophase.

Artifact_Name: Gangetic River Dolphin (Preserved Specimen)
Description: As a popular and newly considered species, this special dolphin has been preserved for conservation. It is found mainly in the rivers of Bangladesh and is also known as Shishu or Shushshuk.

Artifact_Name: Linotype Composing Machine
Provenance_Note: Donated by Ananda Bazar Patrika (Suresh Chandra Majumdar) for Bangla keyboard activation
Description: Before printing, text had to be composed — letters arranged one by one. Ottmar Mergenthaler invented the mechanical typesetting machine. This Linotype machine has a keyboard like a typewriter. The machine casts an entire metal line (slug) by pressing keys. Notable: Suresh Chandra Majumdar of Ananda Bazar Patrika's donation for activating the Bangla keyboard on this machine is unforgettable.

Artifact_Name: Pulley (Simple Machine)
Description: A pulley is a grooved wheel that rotates freely around an axle. A rope hangs on either side of the groove. By tying a heavy object to one end and pulling the other end, the object can be lifted. There are two types of pulley: fixed and movable. A fixed pulley does not give mechanical advantage; it only changes the direction of force. A movable pulley changes both direction and gives mechanical advantage.

Artifact_Name: Radar Antenna & Radar Display
Description: Used to locate aeroplanes, rockets, etc. within a specific area. Detection information is obtained from the display.

Artifact_Name: Ancient Printing Press (Gutenberg-type)
Description: Johann Gutenberg invented the printing machine. He initially carved images on wooden blocks and printed playing cards. He then carved images and brief biographies of great men onto large wooden blocks and printed them. In 1450 CE he opened the first printing press and in 1455 CE the first book (the Bible) was printed. In 1822, Arthur and William Cope Accibian Press made an improved machine, one of which is kept in the Dhaka City Museum. An improved version of that machine from 1893 is now displayed in the Science Museum.

Artifact_Name: Electron Microscope (Model)
Description: Unlike ordinary microscopes that use light, electron microscopes use electrons. An ordinary light microscope can magnify objects up to 2,000 times. A modern electron microscope can magnify objects up to 10,000,000 times. The advantage of the electron microscope is that the wavelength of the electron wave is very short, giving it a much higher magnification power.

Artifact_Name: Balaka Aircraft Jet Engine
Description: In 1972, the Soviet Union gifted a personal aircraft to Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman — the Balaka aircraft. Its engine was donated to the Science Museum by the Bangladesh Air Force in 1991 as a museum exhibit.

Artifact_Name: Ancient Aircraft Engine (WWII Radial Engine)
Description: A 14-cylinder (7 per row, 2 rows) radially connected spark ignition engine with cylinder heads. Each cylinder has two spark plugs. If one plug misses, the other immediately takes over. All pistons' function is to rotate the shaft. The engine was made by Wright Aeronautical Corporation (USA) in 1941. The aircraft was used in World War II.

Artifact_Name: Old Gramophone (Phonograph)
Description: Invented by Thomas Alva Edison. Energy is supplied by winding a spring by hand. When the speaker's pin is placed on the rotating plate, the device starts playing.

Artifact_Name: Engine Air Tourer (Aircraft Training Engine)
Description: A 4-cylinder and cylinder aircraft engine with a shaft and propeller. The aircraft was mainly used for training purposes. Its engine model is RPM-2750.

Artifact_Name: Suspension Bridge Model (Hardinge Bridge)
Description: A model of a suspension bridge, showing how two curved cables connect the main tower to the bridge. Suspension bridge's biggest advantage is that such a long span cannot be achieved by any other bridge type. John Augustus Roebling (German-American engineer) first designed and built a suspension bridge in New York over the East River in 1883, with a main span of 1,595 feet.

Artifact_Name: Lever (Simple Machine Exhibit)
Description: A lever is a simple machine. With it, heavy objects can be lifted with little force. Levers are of three classes depending on the position of fulcrum, force, and load. 1st class: fulcrum between force and load (e.g. see-saw, scissors, hand pump handle). 2nd class: load between fulcrum and force (e.g. wheelbarrow, nutcracker, paper-cutting machine). 3rd class: force applied between fulcrum and load (e.g. tongs, lifting heavy objects with forearm).

Artifact_Name: Video Wkon Camera (Historic Video Camera)
Description: An early video camera on display as part of the Technology Gallery's collection of historic instruments.

Artifact_Name: Newton's Colour Disc
Description: Demonstrates that the light of white colour is a mixture of seven different colours in specific proportions: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red (VIBGYOR). These colours are painted on the disc. When the disc is rotated, due to the inability of human brain perception in too short a time, all colours appear as white.

Artifact_Name: Cinemascope
Description: Demonstrates how cinema works. The human eye cannot detect more than averagely 10 individual pictures per second. If the exposure of pictures is more than 10 per second, the pictures seem to be continuous. This is the theme of motion pictures or movies.

Artifact_Name: Fun Mirrors (Magic Mirrors)
Description: Fun mirrors are different from ordinary mirrors — they are convex and concave. Standing in front of these mirrors, your face appears short, tall, or contracted. This is because the mirrors are (1) convex, (2) concave. Because of being convex and concave, the face appears this way.

Artifact_Name: Multiple Images (Peacock Image Exhibit)
Description: Shows a single image displayed in multiple different ways — called a 'bahurupi' (multiple-image). Looking through the round window of the exhibit toward the framed peacock image and rotating the knob, you can see the colour of the image gradually changing.

Artifact_Name: Severed Head Illusion
Description: Standing in the empty hole of the exhibit, the visitor appears as if their head is cut off and placed on a plate or dish kept in the exhibit.

Artifact_Name: Kaleidoscope
Description: Three flat mirrors arranged inside the tube as the three sides of an equilateral triangle. The reflections of these three mirrors inside the kaleidoscope are at equal angles (60°) to each other. There are three-layered flat triangular transparent containers inside, each layer filled with coloured liquid. Rotating the tube causes the colourful liquid to flow downward while a beautiful changing pattern is formed and reflected repeatedly in the triangular mirrors before the viewer's eyes.

Artifact_Name: Colourful Liquid Patterns
Description: Through various coloured liquids, their density and surface tension can be used to create beautiful patterns.

Artifact_Name: Can Light Be Seen? (Light in Vacuum)
Description: Looking at the switch-type tube from outside, light cannot be seen. But placing a hand inside the tube, the hand appears illuminated. Light can only be seen when an object reflects light to our eyes. This is why the sky appears dark further from Earth's atmosphere.

Artifact_Name: Upward Electric Arc
Description: When the switch is pressed, an upward electric arc is created between two conducting rods by ionisation and lightning discharge. A potential difference of 25,000 volts is applied between the two rods. The arc travels upward due to convection of the hot ionised air.

Artifact_Name: Seebeck Siren
Description: When the disc of the exhibit is turned slowly after switching on, eight separate musical tones are heard one by one.

Artifact_Name: Floating Disc (Electromagnetic Levitation)
Description: Pressing the switch, the disc immediately jumps up and floats in the air — an application of Lenz's law of electromagnetic induction.

Artifact_Name: Iris (Eye Pupil Demonstration)
Description: A circular dark spot can be seen at the exact centre of the eye globe by bringing the face very close to the concave mirror. Rotating the knob changes the brightness of light. The iris works like the aperture control of a camera. In dim light, the iris dilates to allow more light for better visibility.

Artifact_Name: Anamorphosis (Distorted Image Restoration)
Description: A distorted drawn image: looking at the reflection on a cylindrical or conical reflector, the true object can be recognised. This is an application of the linear transformation matrix of non-linear kinematics.

Artifact_Name: Lazy Tongs / Inertia Exhibit
Description: All rods are knocked down through a hole path one by one. Even when all rods fall together, one rod falls with a delay. The exhibit demonstrates how superconductors are formed by the emergence of attraction force.

Artifact_Name: Two Ears Hearing (Binaural Direction Sensing)
Description: Sitting in the exhibit's seat and holding both ear-pieces to both ears, with a companion standing behind and striking various parts of the plastic with a finger, you can tell which direction the sound comes from. Every time you can estimate the source location of the sound. The exhibit explains 'why do we need two ears?'

Artifact_Name: Ancient Petrified Wood
Finding_Place: Lalmai and Mainamati, Comilla District, Bangladesh
Description: One of the most significant objects in the museum; ancient fossilized wood estimated at 2.5 million years old, offering evidence of prehistoric vegetation of Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Whale Skeleton (Giant Whale Saw Fish)
Description: Large skeleton of a giant whale saw fish, one of the notable objects of the natural history galleries. A tongue of a whale is also on separate display.

Artifact_Name: Royal Bengal Tiger (Taxidermied)
Description: Stuffed Royal Bengal Tiger from the Sundarbans mangrove forest, displayed to represent Bangladesh's iconic wildlife. A large statue also displayed separately.

Artifact_Name: Spotted Deer (Chital Deer) Display
Description: Taxidermied Chitral (spotted) deer from the Sundarbans, displayed alongside other wildlife specimens in the natural heritage galleries.

Artifact_Name: Beehive Display
Description: Natural beehive specimen displayed as part of insect and flora collections illustrating the biodiversity of Bangladesh.

Artifact_Name: Butterfly Collection
Description: Collection of different types of butterflies representing the insect biodiversity of Bangladesh, displayed in the natural history section.

Artifact_Name: Reptile Collection
Description: Collection of reptile specimens representing native reptilian fauna of Bangladesh, forming part of the natural history galleries.

Artifact_Name: Sea Life of the Bay of Bengal Collection
Description: Marine specimens representing the biodiversity of the Bay of Bengal and coastal waters, including shells, mollusks, and sea creatures.

Artifact_Name: Rocks and Minerals Collection
Description: Geological specimens including rocks, minerals, and a geological map of Bangladesh illustrating the country's geomorphology.

Artifact_Name: Flora Specimens (Cereals, Pulses, Herbal Medicines)
Description: Collection of economically important plants, cereals, pulses, herbal medicines, flowers, fruits and creepers representing Bangladesh's plant heritage.

Artifact_Name: Bird Collection (Birds of Bangladesh)
Description: Display of various bird species of Bangladesh including migratory and native birds, presented as part of natural heritage galleries with semi-dioramas.

Artifact_Name: Peacock (Peafowl) Specimen
Description: Taxidermied peafowl displayed as part of the bird collection representing Bangladesh's native bird species.

Artifact_Name: Elephant Display
Description: Large elephant display forming a dedicated gallery in the natural history section, showcasing one of the largest land animals found in Bangladesh.

Artifact_Name: Sundarbans Diorama
Description: Semi-diorama and diorama displays depicting the Sundarbans mangrove ecosystem, the world's largest mangrove forest, with its fauna and flora.

Artifact_Name: Monkey and Langur Specimens
Description: Monkey and langur specimens preserved and displayed as part of the natural history mammal collection.

Artifact_Name: Naga Darwaza (Serpent Doorway)
Description: A spectacular black stone serpent doorway (Naga Darwaza), one of the most significant objects in the museum. Represents medieval temple architecture of Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Black Basalt Buddha Statue (Pala Period)
Description: A serene and exquisitely crafted black basalt Buddha statue from the Pala Dynasty period, considered one of the finest examples of ancient Bengali Buddhist art. Features intricate detailing and a calm expression characteristic of Pala School of Art.

Artifact_Name: Tara Statue (Pala Era)
Description: Iconic Pala-era sculpture of the Bodhisattva Tara, a goddess revered in both Buddhism and Hinduism. Renowned as one of the most important sculptures in the museum's collection.

Artifact_Name: Surya (Sun God) Statue – Pala Period
Description: Famous stone sculpture of Surya (the Sun God) from the Pala period, known for its expressive face and intricate carvings, representative of the high artistic tradition of ancient Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Vishnu Statue – Pala Period
Description: Stone sculpture of the Hindu deity Vishnu from the Pala period, a major attraction in the sculpture galleries representing the Hindu artistic and religious tradition of ancient Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Durga Sculpture
Description: Bronze or stone image of the Hindu goddess Durga from the Pala-Sena period, part of the museum's extensive collection of ancient Bengali religious sculptures.

Artifact_Name: Bronze Bodhisattva Figures
Description: Collection of exquisite bronze images of Bodhisattvas from the Pala period, characterized by slender forms, elaborate ornamentation, and serene expressions representing the Pala School of Art.

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Plaques from Mahasthangarh
Period_Dating: Mauryan–Gupta Period (3rd Century BC – 6th Century AD)
Description: Terracotta plaques recovered from Mahasthangarh, one of Bengal's earliest known urban archaeological sites, depicting deities, mythological scenes, and daily life of ancient inhabitants.

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Plaques from Paharpur
Description: Terracotta plaques and architectural fragments excavated from Paharpur (Somapura Mahavihara), a UNESCO World Heritage Site representing the largest Buddhist monastery south of the Himalayas.

Artifact_Name: Prehistoric Hand Axes (Stone Tools)
Description: Iron and stone hand axes and other prehistoric lithic tools representing the earliest human presence in the Bengal region, part of the Stone Age artifact collection.

Artifact_Name: Ancient Pottery Collection
Description: Collection of ancient pottery and ceramics from various periods of Bengal's history, from Neolithic handmade ware to wheel-thrown ceramics of the Sultanate period, representing daily life of ancient peoples.

Artifact_Name: Coins of Emperor Sher Shah (Gold / Silver)
Description: Rare coins minted during the reign of Emperor Sher Shah Suri, one of the most significant medieval rulers of the Indian subcontinent. Part of the museum's vast collection of over 53,000 ancient and medieval coins.

Artifact_Name: Ancient and Medieval Coin Collection (General)
Period_Dating: Mauryan to Mughal Period (3rd BC – 18th AD)
Finding_Place: Various sites across Bengal and India
Description: A vast collection of over 53,000 gold, silver, and copper coins from the Mauryan, Gupta, Pala, Sultanate, and Mughal periods, documenting the monetary and political history of Bengal and the Indian subcontinent.

Artifact_Name: Ancient Stone Inscriptions
Period_Dating: Gupta to Sultanate Period (4th–15th Century AD)
Description: Collection of stone inscriptions in Sanskrit, Arabic, and Persian from various medieval dynasties, providing historical records of rulers, land grants, and religious dedications.

Artifact_Name: Copperplate Inscriptions
Description: Ancient copperplate inscriptions recording royal land grants, administrative decrees, and genealogical records of the Pala and Sena dynasties of Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Surrender Table (16 December 1971)
Description: The historic table on which Lt. General A. A. K. Niazi of the Pakistan Army signed the Instrument of Surrender to the Joint Forces of Bangladesh and India on 16 December 1971, marking Bangladesh's independence.

Artifact_Name: First Flag of Independent Bangladesh (Foreign Mission Copy)
Description: The first flag of independent Bangladesh hoisted at foreign missions, representing a key symbol of national sovereignty during the Liberation War of 1971.

Artifact_Name: 7 March 1971 Declaration (Sheikh Mujibur Rahman)
Description: Historic declaration delivered by Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman on 7 March 1971 at Suhrawardy Udyan, Dhaka – now recognized as a UNESCO World Memory of the World. The museum preserves documents and artifacts related to this speech.

Artifact_Name: Shirt and Shoes of Shaheed Shafiur Rahman
Gallery_No: War of Liberation / Language Movement Gallery
Description: The bullet-ridden and blood-stained shirt and shoes of Shaheed Shafiur Rahman, a martyr of the Language Movement of 21 February 1952, who was killed by police under the Pakistani government.

Artifact_Name: Personal Mementos of Shaheed Asad
Description: Personal mementos and effects belonging to Shaheed Asaduzzaman Asad, a student leader martyred during the Mass Uprising of 1969 against Pakistani rule.

Artifact_Name: Mementos of Kazi Nazrul Islam
Description: Historic mementos, personal effects, and items associated with Kazi Nazrul Islam, the national poet of Bangladesh and revolutionary poet of Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Mementos of Rabindranath Tagore
Description: Historic mementos and memorabilia associated with Rabindranath Tagore, Nobel Laureate poet whose work is deeply intertwined with Bengali cultural identity.

Artifact_Name: Mementos of Michael Madhusudan Dutt
Description: Historical mementos and artifacts associated with Michael Madhusudan Dutt, pioneering Bengali poet and dramatist of the 19th century.

Artifact_Name: Mementos of Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain
Description: Historical mementos of Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain, pioneering feminist writer and social reformer of Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Liberation War Documents and Photographs
Description: Collection of documents, photographs, posters, and records related to the Liberation War of Bangladesh in 1971, including photos of refugee camps, genocide documentation, and freedom fighting activities.

Artifact_Name: Torture Machines (Pakistani Army – 1971)
Description: Torture machines and instruments used by the Pakistani army during the Liberation War of 1971, preserved as evidence of the genocide and war crimes committed against Bengali civilians and freedom fighters.

Artifact_Name: Manuscripts (Palm Leaf and Paper)
Finding_Place: Various monastic and scholarly sites, Bengal
Description: Collection of ancient palm-leaf manuscripts and paper manuscripts written in Sanskrit, Bengali, Arabic, and Persian, representing the intellectual and religious traditions of medieval Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Miniature Paintings Collection
Description: Collection of Mughal-style miniature paintings depicting courtly life, battles, religious themes, and portraits, representing the peak of Indo-Persian artistic tradition in Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Mughal Era Arms and Weapons
Description: Collection of arms and armour from the Mughal era, including swords, shields, daggers, and firearms. The museum holds one of the largest collections of arms and armour in the Indian subcontinent.

Artifact_Name: Old Guns at Entrance (Colonial Era Cannons)
Description: Collection of old guns and cannons displayed at the museum entrance, representing the colonial era military heritage of Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Iron Axes (Prehistoric)
Description: Collection of iron axes from the Iron Age period of Bengal, representing the technological advancement in metalworking among ancient peoples of the region.

Artifact_Name: Medals, Royal Decrees and Historic Artworks
Description: Collection of medals, royal decrees, and historic artworks from various periods representing political authority, honors, and administrative records of Bengal's rulers.

Artifact_Name: Atom Bomb Pieces (Hiroshima and Nagasaki)
Description: Pieces of the atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Japan in August 1945, preserved as a reminder of the devastating effects of nuclear warfare. Also includes potteries burnt during the Second World War.

Artifact_Name: Ancient Potteries burnt in Hiroshima (WWII)
Description: Potteries burnt and damaged during the atomic bomb blast in Hiroshima, Japan in 1945, collected as war artifacts and presented alongside the atom bomb debris.

Artifact_Name: Buddhist and Brahminical Stone Sculptures (General Collection)
Period_Dating: Gupta to Pala-Sena Period (4th–12th Century AD)
Description: Extensive collection of Buddhist and Brahminical stone sculptures from the Gupta, Pala, and Sena periods, representing the zenith of classical Bengali religious art. The world-famous collection is a major attraction for international visitors.

Artifact_Name: Sandstone Sculptures (General Collection)
Description: Collection of sandstone sculptures including Hindu and Buddhist deities, architectural figures, and decorative pieces from the Gupta and Pala periods of Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Architectural Specimens (Temple / Mosque Fragments)
Description: Fascinating ancient architectural specimens including stone carvings, brick motifs, and terracotta architectural decorations from temples, mosques, and monasteries of medieval Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Ivory Mat (Hand-crafted)
Description: An extraordinary and rare mat made entirely from ivory, showcasing the remarkable craftsmanship of Bengali artisans. One of the most unique objects in the museum's collection.

Artifact_Name: Muslin of Dhaka (Jamdani / Dhaka Muslin)
Period_Dating: Mughal to Colonial Period (16th–19th Century AD)
Description: Legendary Dhaka Muslin, often described as 'woven air', representing one of the finest textiles ever produced by human hands. Dhaka muslin was globally renowned during the Mughal era for its extraordinary fineness. The Jamdani weaving tradition is now a UNESCO-recognized Intangible Cultural Heritage.

Artifact_Name: Nakshi Kantha (Embroidered Quilt) Collection
Description: Collection of Nakshi Kantha, traditional embroidered quilts hand-stitched by rural Bengali women, depicting scenes from rural life, folklore, and religious motifs. Each piece is a unique narrative woven into fabric, representing a vibrant tradition of Bangladeshi folk art.

Artifact_Name: Wood Carvings Collection
Description: Extensive collection of intricately carved wooden objects including furniture, architectural panels, household items, and decorative pieces representing the woodworking tradition of Bangladesh and Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Metalwork Collection (Brass, Bronze, Silver)
Description: Collection of decorative metalwork including household utensils, religious objects, decorative vessels, and ornamental pieces made from brass, bronze, silver, and copper, representing Bengal's rich metalworking tradition.

Artifact_Name: Porcelain and Glassware Collection
Description: Collection of porcelain and glassware including Chinese export porcelain, local pottery, and decorative glass objects that were traded and used in Bengal during medieval and colonial times.

Artifact_Name: Ivory Works Collection
Description: Collection of intricate ivory carvings including decorative objects, combs, figurines, and household items, showcasing the exceptional skill of Bengali ivory craftsmen. Also includes objects from royal households.

Artifact_Name: Traditional Musical Instruments
Description: Collection of traditional Bangladeshi and Bengali musical instruments including string, wind, and percussion instruments representing the folk and classical musical traditions of Bangladesh. Includes instruments of various ethnic groups.

Artifact_Name: Dolls Collection (Traditional)
Description: Collection of traditional handmade dolls and figurines from different regions of Bangladesh, representing folk craft traditions and child culture of rural Bengali society.

Artifact_Name: Textiles and Costumes Collection
Description: Collection of traditional textiles and costumes from various regions of Bangladesh, including handwoven fabrics, tribal costumes, ceremonial dress, and everyday attire of different ethnic communities.

Artifact_Name: Tribal Artifacts – Tribes of Bangladesh
Finding_Place: Chittagong Hill Tracts and other regions, Bangladesh
Description: Extensive collection of ethnographic objects from various indigenous ethnic groups of Bangladesh (Chakma, Marma, Tripura, Garo, Santal, etc.) including household tools, ceremonial objects, traditional weapons, housing models, and cultural items.

Artifact_Name: Boats of Bangladesh (Miniature Models)
Description: Collection of miniature and model traditional boats representing the diverse boat-building heritage of Bangladesh, a riverine delta nation. Includes various types of sailing and rowing boats that have largely vanished from modern use.

Artifact_Name: Household Objects and Daily Life Exhibits
Description: Collection of everyday household objects representing rural and urban domestic life in Bangladesh, including cooking utensils, farming tools, fishing implements, and household furniture of different socioeconomic groups.

Artifact_Name: Arms and Weapons of Ethnic Groups
Finding_Place: Chittagong Hill Tracts and other regions
Description: Traditional weapons and arms used by various ethnic communities of Bangladesh for hunting, defense, and ceremonial purposes, including bows, arrows, spears, dao (machetes), and traditional firearms.

Artifact_Name: Customs and Ceremonies Objects
Description: Objects used in customs, ceremonies, and rituals of different ethnic communities of Bangladesh, representing the diverse ceremonial traditions and belief systems of the nation's indigenous peoples.

Artifact_Name: Jewellery Collection
Description: Collection of traditional jewellery and ornaments from various regions and communities of Bangladesh, including gold, silver, and bronze ornaments representing different socioeconomic backgrounds and ethnic traditions.

Artifact_Name: Famine Sketches of 1943 by Zainul Abedin
Description: The landmark sketches depicting the devastating Bengal Famine of 1943 by Shilpacharya Zainul Abedin, one of the most significant artworks in the museum. These sketches bear testimony to the miserable condition of people suffering from starvation and are considered national treasures.

Artifact_Name: Paintings by Potua Quamrul Hassan
Description: Famous contemporary paintings by Potua Quamrul Hassan, a pioneering Bangladeshi painter and graphic designer known for his distinctive folk-inspired style and political artwork, including anti-Pakistani army posters during the 1971 Liberation War.

Artifact_Name: Paintings by SM Sultan
Description: Celebrated paintings by SM Sultan (Sheikh Muhammad Sultan), renowned Bangladeshi painter known for his monumental depictions of rural Bengal, its laborers, and river life, often featuring muscular peasants as central figures.

Artifact_Name: European Art Reproductions (Renaissance to Modern)
Description: Collection of famous European artworks from the Renaissance to the Modern period, including reproductions of masterpieces from major European art galleries, providing visitors with a window into global art history.

Artifact_Name: Portraits of World Personalities
Description: Large collection of portraits of internationally renowned politicians, artists, scientists, and historical figures from around the world, displayed on the third floor of the museum.

Artifact_Name: Portraits of National Heroes of Bangladesh
Description: Collection of portraits and photographs of Bangladeshi national heroes, freedom fighters, and martyred intellectuals representing those who shaped the nation's history and independence.

Artifact_Name: Bangabhaban Collection (Local and Foreign Objects)
Description: Various local and foreign objects collected from Bangabhaban (the Presidential Palace), including gifts received from foreign dignitaries and state objects of historical and diplomatic significance.

Artifact_Name: Korean Gallery – Korean Cultural Artifacts
Description: Collection of Korean cultural artifacts, artworks, and cultural objects gifted by Korea as part of bilateral cultural exchange, representing Korean heritage and artistry.

Artifact_Name: Chinese Gallery – Chinese Cultural Artifacts
Description: Collection of Chinese cultural objects, artworks, and artifacts representing China's rich civilization, displayed as part of the museum's World Civilization section and gifted through diplomatic cultural exchange.

Artifact_Name: Iranian Gallery – Iranian Cultural Artifacts
Description: Collection of Iranian cultural artifacts and artworks representing Persian civilization, including metalwork, calligraphy, and decorative arts, displayed as part of the museum's world civilization section.

Artifact_Name: Swiss Gallery – Swiss Cultural Artifacts
Description: Collection of Swiss cultural objects and artifacts representing Swiss heritage and artistry, displayed as part of the international collections on the third floor.

Artifact_Name: Language Movement of 1952 Artifacts
Description: Collection of documents, photographs, personal effects, and artifacts related to the Language Movement of 21 February 1952, when Bengali students and activists were killed demanding recognition of Bangla as the state language. Includes personal items of martyrs.

Artifact_Name: Folk Art and Crafts Collection
Description: Collection of traditional folk art and crafts from various regions of Bangladesh including pottery, wooden dolls, bamboo crafts, jute products, and festival-related artworks representing the rich folk artistic tradition of the country.

Artifact_Name: Festival Masks
Description: Traditional festival masks used in cultural festivals, rituals, and folk performances across Bangladesh, representing the artistic and ceremonial traditions of various communities.

Artifact_Name: Sculptures in Art Corners (Diverse Nations)
Description: Collection of sculptures from home and abroad displayed in the four corners of the Contemporary Art and World Civilization department, including artworks donated by various countries.

Artifact_Name: Indra (Guardian of the East)
Finding_Place: Central Temple Basement, Somapura Mahavihara, Paharpur, Naogaon
Description: Indra, lord of heaven and guardian of the eastern quarter, stands in Samapada pose before his vehicle Airavata the elephant. Originally installed in a niche in the south-eastern section of the temple's basement wall (niche no. 29). He has two arms, an ornate halo, and holds a small round object. The figure wears a pleated loincloth, chain girdle, twisted necklace, armlets and an ornate jatamukuta crown. His forehead bears a horizontal third eye. First misidentified by Dikshit as connected to Krishna legend; later confirmed as Indra, guardian of the east. Accession no. S-4. (Source: Ahmed & Kabir 2016, PDF3)

Artifact_Name: Krishna Killing the Demon Keśin
Finding_Place: Central Temple Basement, Somapura Mahavihara, Paharpur, Naogaon
Description: Young Krishna charges the horse-shaped demon Keśin by thrusting his left elbow into the animal's jaws while the fallen demon (in human form) lies under his left foot. Originally fixed on the south-east wall of the central temple (niche no. 30). Krishna wears a lower garment with chain girdle and has a distinctive kakapaksha (crow-wing) hairstyle. Flanked by plantain trees. Initially misidentified by Dikshit as Dhenuka-badha; corrected by Saraswati. Accession no. A-6. (Source: Ahmed & Kabir 2016, PDF3)

Artifact_Name: Vāyu (God of Wind)
Finding_Place: Central Temple Basement, Somapura Mahavihara, Paharpur, Naogaon
Description: Vāyu, god of wind and guardian of the northwestern quarter, stands in samapadasthanaka pose. His head is framed by an inflated shawl — the distinctive sign of Vāyu in Eastern Indian iconography — the ends of which he holds symmetrically. Flanked by two small attendants, one male and one female, with similar fluttering shawls. Originally positioned on the southern basement wall (niche no. 39). Mistakenly identified by Dikshit and Saraswati as Yama due to its southern position; later correctly identified as Vāyu. Accession no. 1. (Source: Ahmed & Kabir 2016, PDF3)

Artifact_Name: Chandra (Moon God)
Finding_Place: Central Temple Basement, Somapura Mahavihara, Paharpur, Naogaon
Description: Chandra, the moon god, stands in samapadasthanaka pose on a projecting pedestal between two plantain trees. He wears a long loincloth and a broad vastropavita on his chest, with no other ornaments. His long hair is arranged in a jatamukuta above which is shown a large lying crescent moon. The right hand holds an akshamala (rosary) and the lowered left holds a small kamandalu (water pot). Originally in the north-western section of the temple (niche no. 60). First identified as Shiva by Dikshit; corrected by Saraswati as Chandra. (Source: Ahmed & Kabir 2016, PDF3)

Artifact_Name: Balarāma Avatāra
Finding_Place: Central Temple Basement, Somapura Mahavihara, Paharpur, Naogaon
Description: Balarāma, the elder brother of Krishna, represented as an avatāra standing on a plain pedestal with a slight bend (abhanga). Over his head is a seven-hooded snake canopy. Has four hands: upper right and left hold a pestle and ploughshare; lower right holds a wine cup; left hand is akimbo. Accompanied by male and female attendants, the female holding a wine flask and cup. Originally positioned alongside images of Krishna, Radha and Yamuna on the south-facing long wall (niche no. 24). Shows influence of Late Gupta tradition in ornaments. Accession no. 2. (Source: Ahmed & Kabir 2016, PDF3)

Artifact_Name: Subhadrā-haraṇa (Arjuna Abducting Subhadrā)
Finding_Place: Central Temple Basement, Somapura Mahavihara, Paharpur, Naogaon
Description: A narrative panel depicting two divine figures with halos, both holding bows with arrows drawn at each other. The figure on the left (Krishna on Garuda) faces the one on the right (Arjuna on a chariot, two wheels visible in profile). A female figure (Subhadrā) bows low in fear. The scene depicts Arjuna's abduction of Subhadrā (Krishna's sister) with Krishna staging a mock fight to protect Balarāma's ego. Originally on the southern end of the main western wall (niche no. 54). Accession no. S-8. (Source: Ahmed & Kabir 2016, PDF3)

Artifact_Name: Vasudeva and Devaki with Baby Krishna in Kaṃsa's Prison
Finding_Place: Central Temple Basement, Somapura Mahavihara, Paharpur, Naogaon
Description: A narrative stone relief depicting Vasudeva and Devaki (Krishna's parents) in Kaṃsa's prison with baby Krishna. The panel belongs to the series of Krishna's early life stories which are the dominant subject matter of the Paharpur temple sculptures. This scene depicts the moment of Krishna's miraculous birth in the prison of his evil uncle Kaṃsa. From the 3rd group (8th century CE) of Saraswati's classification representing the indigenous Eastern Indian artistic tradition. (Source: Ahmed & Kabir 2016, PDF3)

Artifact_Name: Gaṇeśa
Finding_Place: Central Temple Basement, Somapura Mahavihara, Paharpur, Naogaon
Description: A sandstone sculpture of Gaṇeśa, the elephant-headed Hindu deity and remover of obstacles, recovered from the basement wall of the Paharpur central temple. One of only three Gaṇeśa sculptures among the 63 stone sculptures at Paharpur. His presence is linked to Tantric Vajrayana Buddhist practice which incorporated Brahmanical deities in outer mandala positions around the main Buddhist shrine. (Source: Ahmed & Kabir 2016, PDF3)

Artifact_Name: Kīrtimukha (Face of Glory)
Description: A stone image of Kīrtimukha — the 'face of glory', a fierce leonine face used as an auspicious guardian motif above doorways and in temple decoration in Hindu and Buddhist traditions. The Kīrtimukha is associated with Śiva and also appears in the terracotta plaques of Paharpur. Accession no. listed in the museum as 5th–6th century CE. (Source: Ahmed & Kabir 2016, PDF3)

Artifact_Name: Nāga / Door Jamb with Chakrapuruṣa
Finding_Place: Central Temple Basement, Somapura Mahavihara, Paharpur, Naogaon
Description: Currently labelled as 'Nāga' in the museum, Dr. Enamul Haque has identified this sculpture as a door jamb depicting Chakrapuruṣa (personification of the wheel/discus of Viṣṇu). The mislabelling illustrates the ongoing debate about iconographic identification of the Paharpur sculptures. An important example of the museum's need for updated scholarly labels. (Source: Ahmed & Kabir 2016, PDF3)

Artifact_Name: Dancing Female Figure
Finding_Place: Central Temple Basement, Somapura Mahavihara, Paharpur, Naogaon
Description: One of four panels depicting female dancing figures found at the Paharpur temple basement. These figures represent the free-flowing, dynamic positions of classical dance and belong to Saraswati's third group (8th century CE) — the undiluted indigenous Eastern Indian artistic tradition. Their lively compositions represent an art style seldom found in stone but common in terracotta, characteristic of the Paharpur artistic school. (Source: Ahmed & Kabir 2016, PDF3)

Artifact_Name: Part of a Stela — Flying Vidyādhara
Description: Part of a stela showing a flying Vidyādhara — a celestial being in Hindu and Buddhist mythology who possesses magical knowledge (vidyā). Vidyādharas are depicted flying through the air, often carrying garlands. This fragment is a rare example of this iconographic type in the Paharpur sculptural corpus and attests to the cosmopolitan mythological vocabulary shared by Buddhist and Brahmanical traditions in medieval Bengal. (Source: Ahmed & Kabir 2016, PDF3)

Artifact_Name: Hevajra with Śakti (Fragmentary)
Finding_Place: Eastern Wing — Monk's Cell, Somapura Mahavihara, Paharpur, Naogaon
Description: Fragmentary image of Hevajra — a male Tantric deity — in passionate embrace with his Śakti (the personification of divine feminine creative power). Described by World Heritage Journeys Europe as one of the finest items in the Paharpur Museum collection and by Lonely Planet as 'the finest item in the collection'. The image attests to the Vajrayana Tantric Buddhist practice at Paharpur. Belongs to the later phase (10th–11th century CE) of Paharpur's occupation. (Sources: Ahmed & Kabir 2016; World Heritage Journeys; Lonely Planet)

Artifact_Name: Kubera (Seated, God of Wealth)
Description: A seated image of Kubera, the Hindu and Buddhist god of wealth, displayed at the Paharpur Museum. In the Paharpur temple, Kubera appears as a Dikpāla (guardian of a cardinal direction — the north). The reverse side of another sculpture at Paharpur shows a defaced face of Kubera, suggesting possible reuse of earlier sculptural material. One of very few independent Kubera images from Paharpur. (Source: Ahmed & Kabir 2016, PDF3)

Artifact_Name: Colossal Bronze Buddha (Torso Fragment)
Finding_Place: Eastern Wing — Monk's Cell 37, Somapura Mahavihara, Paharpur, Naogaon
Description: A fragment of a colossal standing bronze Buddha — the upper body and head — discovered in cell 37 of the eastern wing, buried upside down under the second floor of the late phase of the monastery. The full image is estimated to have been approximately 240 cm high, making it the largest standing bronze image in Bengal. The rounded face shows urna, half-closed eyes, full lips, elongated earlobes, ushnisa and small snail curls. Reminiscent of Classical Gupta art. According to Lonely Planet this image is 'usually away on a seemingly endless world tour.' (Sources: Ahmed & Kabir 2016; Lonely Planet; Wikipedia)

Artifact_Name: Bronze Buddha Bust (Medium)
Description: A medium-sized bronze bust of a Buddha — one of the principal collections of the Paharpur Museum listed on Wikipedia. Along with the colossal bronze torso, this bust represents the Buddhist bronze-casting tradition at Paharpur under the Pāla dynasty. Stucco Buddha heads unearthed at Paharpur are similar to the Gandhāra style of Indo-Hellenic sculpture. (Sources: Wikipedia; Lonely Planet)

Artifact_Name: Hāragaurī (Decorated Metal, Damaged)
Description: A damaged decorated metal image of Hāragaurī — the composite form of Śiva (Hara) and Pārvatī (Gaurī). Listed among the notable preserved statues in the Paharpur Museum on Wikipedia. Though damaged, this piece attests to the Brahmanical sculptural tradition at Paharpur alongside the dominant Buddhist iconographic programme. (Source: Wikipedia)

Artifact_Name: Nude Jain Idol (Bronze)
Description: A nude Jain idol (Tīrthankara in kāyotsarga — the standing meditation posture) in bronze. Listed among the notable metal statues of the Paharpur Museum on Wikipedia. The presence of Jain bronzes at Paharpur is consistent with the copper plate grant mentioning the Jaina Vihāra of Guhanandin at Vatagohali during 478–479 CE, confirming the multi-religious character of the Paharpur area. (Source: Wikipedia; Ahmed & Kabir 2016)

Artifact_Name: Sandstone Brahma (God of Creation)
Description: A sandstone sculpture of Brahma, the Hindu god of creation, dated to the 10th–11th century CE. Described by World Heritage Journeys Europe as part of the Paharpur collection with caption 'Sandstone sculpture of God Brahma (10th–11th century CE) displayed at Paharpur Museum'. The piece belongs to the later phase of the Paharpur site's occupation and represents the continued Brahmanical religious presence at the site into the Post-Pāla period. (Source: World Heritage Journeys Europe)

Artifact_Name: Bodhisattva Padmapāṇi (Stone Relief)
Period_Dating: c. early Pāla period (8th–9th century CE)
Finding_Place: Central Temple — South Middle Wall, Somapura Mahavihara, Paharpur, Naogaon
Description: The only sculpture on the Paharpur temple surface with definite Buddhist association besides the Nativity of Buddha panel. The god stands in rigid samapadasthanaka pose with left hand holding a lotus by the stalk; the right hand (broken) was probably in varada mudrā. Two mutilated attendant figures flank the deity. Head surrounded by a lotus halo; stela rounded at top with ornamental borders. Originally on the middle of the southern wall; a masonry kunda was built in front of it indicating special veneration. A later insertion into the temple wall. (Source: Ahmed & Kabir 2016, PDF3)

Artifact_Name: Nativity of Buddha at Lumbinī (Stone Relief)
Finding_Place: Central Temple — South-Western Wall, Somapura Mahavihara, Paharpur, Naogaon
Description: One of only two Buddhist iconographic representations on the Paharpur temple wall. The panel (niche no. 52, south-western wall) depicts a woman standing with crossed legs grasping branches of a tree — Queen Māyā at the moment of the Buddha's birth in the Lumbinī garden — with a child to her right and a man beside her. S.K. Saraswati noted compositional affinity with the classic Lumbinī nativity scene. The only representations of Buddhist iconography amidst the predominantly Brahmanical sculptural programme. (Source: Ahmed & Kabir 2016, PDF3)

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Plaques — Cattle Images (Collection, 6 pieces at Mainamati Museum)
Finding_Place: Salban Vihāra / Bhoja Vihāra / Ananda Vihāra / Ranir Bungalow Temple, Paharpur & Mainamati
Description: Out of 2,944 terracotta plaques studied by Uddin (2022), 29 depict cattle. Those from Paharpur sites include: 17 from Somapura Mahavihara (12 in store, 3 in situ in temple, 1 in Varendra Research Museum); 6 from Salban Vihāra (3 in Mainamati Museum, 2 in situ, 1 in Bangladesh National Museum); 1 from Ananda Vihāra; 3 from Bhoja Vihāra; 2 from Ranir Bungalow Temple. Subjects include cows grazing, moving, with calves, resting, grooming, in narrative (Krishna) scenes; bulls charging, moving, in story; buffaloes grazing, moving, dancing, in story. (Source: Uddin 2022, PDF1)

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Plaque — Cow in Grazing Posture (3 pieces)
Description: Three terracotta plaques showing a cow in grazing posture (right lateral view) from Somapura Mahavihara. One shows the cow with a long horn; two others have comparatively short horns. The artist depicts the physique of the cow realistically — dewclaw and hoofs carved perfectly. On one plaque (Fig. 3) body hair of the cow is depicted with etched scratch marks. Currently preserved in the Paharpur Museum Store. (Source: Uddin 2022, PDF1)

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Plaque — Cow and Calf
Provenance_Note: Varendra Research Museum, Rajshahi (Cow & Calf); In Situ (Calf alone)
Description: A beautiful terracotta plaque from Somapura Mahavihara depicting a cow with a calf beside her — both facing left with heads turned back and front legs uplifted, appearing to run and look back with fear. A separate plaque depicting only a jumping calf with all four legs in the air is now in situ in the temple wall at Paharpur. The cow-and-calf plaque is now at Varendra Research Museum, Rajshahi. (Source: Uddin 2022, PDF1)

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Plaque — Ploughing Cow (Ranir Bungalow)
Description: One extraordinary plaque from Ranir Bungalow Temple, Mainamati (the northernmost site in the Lalmai-Mainamati region), showing a man ploughing the field with two cows. The cows have a wooden yoke barrier and pull a hook-shaped plough. The farmer stands behind holding the grip with his left hand and striking the cow's back with his right hand. This is the only terracotta plaque from Bangladesh depicting ploughing and agricultural tools from the 8th–11th centuries CE. (Source: Uddin 2022, PDF1)

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Plaque — Krishna Riding Cow (Cow in Story)
Provenance_Note: In situ position in temple wall, Kotbari, Comilla District
Description: A terracotta plaque from a newly excavated temple of Salban Vihāra depicting young Krishna (Gana Gopāla) riding on a cow. Krishna holds a flute in his right hand and touches the cow with his left. The cow has big horns, is saddled with cloth and has a garland on its neck, depicted in a moving gesture with an upraised tail. Four half-lotus-shaped designs decorate the four corners of the plaque. The 'Kaka-paksha' (crow-wing) hairstyle identifies Krishna. (Source: Uddin 2022, PDF1)

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Plaque — Moving Bull (at National Museum)
Description: A terracotta plaque from the Mainamati region depicting a muscular bull with artistic excellence comparable to a fine sculpture. Half of the plaque is broken away. The remaining portion shows a bull with perfectly carved sharp horns, muzzle, wide nostril and dewlap. This piece is now on permanent display at the Bangladesh National Museum, Dhaka, where it stands as one of the finest examples of animal depiction in Bangladeshi terracotta art. (Source: Uddin 2022, PDF1)

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Plaque — Buffalo in Dancing Posture
Description: One attractive terracotta plaque from Somapura Mahavihara showing a buffalo dancing on its hind legs. The entire body of the buffalo is decorated with pointed marks and rope-like striped marks on the neck. Two twisted horns, small ears and two well-decorated rounded eyes depict the dancing buffalo's image. The unusual dancing posture suggests a narrative story context. (Source: Uddin 2022, PDF1)

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Plaque — Buffalo in Story (Archer Riding Buffalo)
Description: A terracotta plaque from Ranir Bungalow Temple, Mainamati, showing a buffalo carrying a rider. The upper part of the plaque is broken away. The remaining portion shows an archer riding the buffalo (traces of the bow visible) with another archer standing on the ground beside the buffalo, holding a bow. The wide nostril, visible tongue and protrusion of eyes show the aggressive mood of the buffalo. This may depict a battle scene story. (Source: Uddin 2022, PDF1)

Artifact_Name: Cāmuṇḍā (Sandstone)
Description: A sandstone Cāmuṇḍā statue — the fierce form of the goddess among the Saptamātrkā (seven mother goddesses) — listed among the notable preserved statues at Paharpur Museum. Cāmuṇḍā is depicted in her emaciated terrifying form. The presence of Śākta goddess images alongside Buddhist and Vaiṣṇava sculptures attests to the syncretic religious environment at Somapura Mahavihara. (Source: Wikipedia)

Artifact_Name: Standing Śītalā (Red Stone)
Description: A standing image of Śītalā, the Bengali folk goddess of smallpox and cooling diseases, made of red stone. Listed among the notable preserved statues at Paharpur Museum on Wikipedia. Śītalā's presence here reflects the folk and popular religious traditions that existed alongside mainstream Buddhism and Brahmanical religion at Paharpur. (Source: Wikipedia)

Artifact_Name: Viṣṇu Fragment (Black Stone)
Description: A fragment of a Viṣṇu image made of black stone, listed among the notable preserved statues at Paharpur Museum. Vishnu images are notably absent from the 63 stone sculptures originally attached to the Paharpur temple, making this fragment — found elsewhere during excavation — an important addition to understanding the full religious scope of the site. (Source: Wikipedia; Ahmed & Kabir 2016)

Artifact_Name: Standing Gaṇeśa (Black Stone)
Description: A standing Gaṇeśa image made of black stone, listed among the notable preserved statues at Paharpur Museum. Distinct from the sandstone Gaṇeśa on the temple wall, this black stone piece was likely found elsewhere during excavation. Gaṇeśa was one of the most popular Hindu deities incorporated into the Vajrayana Buddhist mandala at Paharpur. (Source: Wikipedia)

Artifact_Name: Broken Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa (Black Stone)
Description: A broken statue of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa (Viṣṇu with his consort Lakṣmī) made of black stone, listed among the notable preserved statues at Paharpur Museum. This Vaiṣṇava composite image represents the union of Viṣṇu and Lakṣmī; the broken state suggests damage from the invasions and destructions the Paharpur monastery suffered over its history. (Source: Wikipedia)

Artifact_Name: Umā (Black Stone)
Description: An Umā (Pārvatī) statue made of black stone, listed among the notable preserved statues at Paharpur Museum. Umā is the principal consort of Śiva and her image attests to the Śaiva tradition at Paharpur. Several Śiva sculptures are found on the temple wall while Umā-Maheśvara and Hāra-Gaurī composite forms are notably absent from the original 63 sculptures, making this separate Umā image significant. (Source: Wikipedia; Ahmed & Kabir 2016)

Artifact_Name: Gaurī (Sandstone)
Description: A Gaurī (another name for Pārvatī, the white/fair goddess) image made of sandstone, listed among the notable preserved statues at Paharpur Museum. Gaurī represents the benevolent aspect of the goddess as the consort of Śiva. (Source: Wikipedia)

Artifact_Name: Viṣṇu (Sandstone)
Description: A sandstone Viṣṇu statue, listed among the notable preserved statues at Paharpur Museum. Depicted with his characteristic four attributes — conch (śaṅkha), discus (cakra), mace (gadā), and lotus (padma). During the Pāla period the worship of Viṣṇu was at its highest level in Bengal, making Vaiṣṇava images particularly significant for this period. (Source: Wikipedia; Ahmed & Kabir 2016)

Artifact_Name: Nandī (Sandstone)
Description: A sandstone Nandī statue — the sacred bull and vehicle of Śiva — listed among the notable preserved statues at Paharpur Museum. A Nandī image in context with Śiva and related images reflects the Śaiva religious practice at and around Paharpur. (Source: Wikipedia)

Artifact_Name: Sūrya (Sandstone)
Description: A sandstone Sūrya (sun god) statue listed among the notable preserved statues at Paharpur Museum. Sūrya images are notably absent from the original 63 sculptures on the temple wall (Ahmed & Kabir 2016 note this), making this separately excavated sandstone piece an important addition to understanding the broader religious iconography of the Paharpur site. (Source: Wikipedia; Ahmed & Kabir 2016)

Artifact_Name: Śivaliṅga (Black Stone)
Description: A Śivaliṅga made of black stone, listed among the notable preserved statues at Paharpur Museum. The Śivaliṅga is the primary aniconic symbol of Lord Śiva in Hindu worship. Its presence at a predominantly Buddhist site reflects the religious syncretism of medieval Bengal where Buddhist and Brahmanical traditions coexisted. (Source: Wikipedia)

Artifact_Name: Manasā (Sandstone)
Description: A sandstone Manasā (serpent goddess) statue, listed among the notable preserved statues at Paharpur Museum. Manasā is noted as absent from the original 63 temple-wall sculptures (Ahmed & Kabir 2016 observe that popular Hindu cults like Manasā were intentionally avoided in the temple decoration). This separately excavated sandstone Manasā reflects the folk religious traditions of the region. (Source: Wikipedia; Ahmed & Kabir 2016)

Artifact_Name: Copper & Silver Coins Collection (8th–16th century)
Description: A collection of old copper and silver coins from the 8th to 16th centuries CE, listed among the collections of the Paharpur Museum on Wikipedia. These span the Pāla, Sena, Sultanate and early Mughal periods, providing a continuous numismatic sequence documenting the history of Paharpur and north Bengal. The coins provide chronological evidence for the long occupation of the site. (Source: Wikipedia)

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Seals & Sealings
Description: A collection of terracotta seals and sealings from Paharpur excavations. Two inscriptions — one copper plate grant and one terracotta sealing — mention religious establishments at the site. Terracotta sealings from Nalanda also mention monks from Somapura, confirming the network between these major Buddhist institutions. The sealings show the Buddhist 'wheel of law' flanked by two deer in the upper register with inscription below. (Source: Ahmed & Kabir 2016, PDF3)

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Amulets & Minor Clay Objects
Description: A collection of terracotta amulets and other minor clay objects listed among the Paharpur Museum collections on Wikipedia, including truncated cone-shaped daggers, flat discs, cylindrical beads, stepped pyramids, lotus petals, chessboard patterns and oblong medals with half-bloomed lotuses. These objects provide evidence of the daily religious and material life of the monks and the lay community at Paharpur. (Source: Wikipedia)

Artifact_Name: Decorated & Ornamental Bricks
Description: A collection of decorated and ornamental bricks from the Paharpur monastery complex, listed among the main collections of the Paharpur Museum. The central temple's three-tier walls were decorated with carved brick cornices, friezes of terracotta plaques and stone sculptures. The ornamental bricks show intricate patterns including floral, geometric and architectural motifs that are characteristic of the Pāla period architectural tradition. (Sources: Wikipedia; UNESCO; Rahman & Nipa 2017, PDF2)

Artifact_Name: Pottery Collection (Various Types)
Description: A collection of pottery and ceramics from Paharpur covering the pre-Pāla, Pāla, and Islamic periods, listed among the main collections of the Paharpur Museum. Includes a variety of vessel types used by the monastery's monk community. One room of the monastery revealed big lumps of charcoal — remains of palm wood used as roof rafter — destroyed in a fire attack by Vangala forces mentioned in the Nalanda inscription. (Sources: Wikipedia; Ahmed & Kabir 2016)

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Female Figurines & Animal Portraits
Description: A collection of terracotta female figurines and animal portraits (separate from the architectonic temple plaques) listed among the Paharpur Museum collections. The animal portraits include depictions of various fauna from the Paharpur region. The female figurines include both religious and secular subjects, adding to the understanding of daily life and religious practice at the medieval monastery. (Source: Wikipedia)

Artifact_Name: Oil Painting — Queen of Dubalhāṭi
Description: An oil painting of the Queen of Dubalhāṭi estate, listed among the notable preserved items at Paharpur Museum. This painting provides historical context for the local aristocratic patronage and history of the Naogaon region in the 19th–20th century. The Dubalhāṭi estate was one of the significant zamindari estates in the Naogaon district. (Source: Wikipedia)

Artifact_Name: Stone Head of Bodhisattva
Description: A loose stone head of a Bodhisattva discovered during Dikshit's excavation, belonging to the 10th–11th century CE. It indicates the continuity of Buddhism in the Paharpur establishment well into the later Pāla period. Along with a fragmentary image of Hevajra with Śakti, a mutilated torso of a Bodhisattva, and a standing female figure of Tārā from the same period. (Source: Ahmed & Kabir 2016, PDF3)

Artifact_Name: Standing Female Figure of Tārā (Stone)
Description: A loose standing female figure of Tārā (Buddhist goddess) discovered at Paharpur. Along with the Bodhisattva head and Hevajra fragment, this 10th–11th century piece indicates the continued importance of Vajrayana Buddhist practice at Paharpur well into the later Pāla period. The only Buddhist Bodhisattva sculpture fixed on the Paharpur temple wall is Padmapāṇi, making this loose Tārā an important supplement to the Buddhist iconographic record of the site. (Source: Ahmed & Kabir 2016, PDF3)

Artifact_Name: Cart Made of Ivory
Description: An antique cart crafted from ivory, part of the state gifts displayed in the Toshakhana Museum

Artifact_Name: Fragment of the Moon Rock
Description: A fragment of lunar rock, gifted to Bangladesh as a diplomatic present, representing international scientific cooperation

Artifact_Name: Various State Crests and Souvenirs
Description: Collection of crests, plaques, and souvenirs gifted to the President and Prime Minister of Bangladesh by foreign dignitaries and governments

Artifact_Name: Fountain – Front Plaza
Description: Decorative fountain at the front plaza of the Bangladesh Military Museum, serving as a welcoming landmark

Artifact_Name: Outdoor Sculptures / Art Installations
Description: Artistic sculptures and installations placed in the outdoor area of the museum, representing military heritage and national pride

Artifact_Name: Jina Ṛṣabhanātha
Description: Jain Tirthankara Ṛṣabhanātha (also called Ādinātha), the first of the 24 Tirthankaras, depicted in meditation posture (dhyana mudra). One of the rare Jain sculptures in the VRM collection.

Artifact_Name: Gaṅgā
Description: Sculpture of Gaṅgā, the Hindu goddess personifying the sacred Ganges river. She is typically shown standing on her vehicle the Makara (crocodile), holding a water pot. This is one of the tallest pieces in the collection.

Artifact_Name: Standing Buddha
Description: A standing Buddha figure from the early Gupta period (5th century CE), one of the oldest sculptures in the collection. The figure displays the characteristic Gupta-period treatment of drapery and facial serenity.

Artifact_Name: Ṣaḍakṣarī Lokeśvara
Description: Seated Bodhisattva Lokeśvara in his six-syllable (Ṣaḍakṣarī) form, associated with the mantra 'Om Mani Padme Hum'. A Mahayana Buddhist deity of compassion from the Pāla period.

Artifact_Name: Mañjuśrī, standing
Description: Standing gilt bronze figure of Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva of wisdom. One of the earliest metal sculptures in the collection, dating to the 7th century CE. Mañjuśrī holds a sword symbolising the cutting of ignorance.

Artifact_Name: Mañjuvara (seated)
Description: Seated form of Mañjuvara, a Buddhist deity closely related to Mañjuśrī. The figure is depicted in a ritual seated posture typical of Pāla-period stone sculptures from the Naogaon region.

Artifact_Name: Khadirāvanī Tārā
Provenance_Note: Sister Christiana (from Miss Margaret Nobel's personal collection)
Description: Tārā in her Khadirāvanī ('of the khadira forest') form, a revered female Bodhisattva of compassion in Vajrayana Buddhism. Notably donated from the personal collection of Sister Nivedita (Margaret Nobel), associate of Swami Vivekananda.

Artifact_Name: Mārīcī
Description: Mārīcī, the Buddhist goddess of the dawn and light, depicted with multiple arms in the Pāla sculptural tradition. She is associated with invisibility and protection from danger.

Artifact_Name: Varāha
Description: Varāha, the boar avatar (third avatāra) of Viṣṇu, depicted rescuing the earth goddess Bhūdevī from the primordial ocean. A quintessential Vaiṣṇava iconographic subject.

Artifact_Name: Twin Garuḍa
Description: A rare twin Garuḍa sculpture — two Garuḍa figures joined together. Garuḍa is the divine eagle-vehicle of Viṣṇu in Hindu mythology. The twin form is uncommon and of significant iconographic interest.

Artifact_Name: Garuḍa
Description: Single Garuḍa figure, the mythical eagle-vehicle of Viṣṇu, shown in the characteristic posture with wings spread and hands in añjali mudrā. Found in Maldah District, West Bengal, India.

Artifact_Name: Sūrya
Description: Early 7th century sculpture of Sūrya, the Hindu solar deity, depicted holding lotus flowers in both hands and wearing northern-style boots (udīcya veṣa). One of the earliest Sūrya images in the collection.

Artifact_Name: Sūrya
Description: A 9th century Pāla-period Sūrya sculpture showing the sun god with elaborate iconographic detail including attendant figures Daṇḍa and Pingala. Representative of the mature Pāla sculptural style.

Artifact_Name: Sūrya
Description: 11th century Sūrya sculpture with characteristic Pāla period iconography — the god shown flanked by female bow-wielders (Daṇḍa and Pingala) and standing on a chariot driven by seven horses.

Artifact_Name: Śiva
Description: Sculpture of Lord Śiva standing in tribhaṅga posture with his characteristic attributes including the crescent moon, trident (triśūla), and damaru drum. Late Pāla period craftsmanship.

Artifact_Name: Śiva Ardhanārī (The half-female lord)
Description: Ardhanārīśvara — the androgynous composite form of Śiva (right half) and Pārvatī/Umā (left half). This iconographic form symbolises the inseparable unity of male and female cosmic principles in Hindu philosophy.

Artifact_Name: Navadurgā
Description: Navadurgā — the nine forms of the goddess Durgā — depicted together in a single sculptural panel. The nine forms include Śailaputrī, Brahmacāriṇī, Candraghaṇṭā, Kūṣmāṇḍā, Skandamātā, Kātyāyanī, Kālarātrī, Mahāgaurī, and Siddhidātrī.

Artifact_Name: Durgā Mahiṣamardinī
Description: Durgā slaying the buffalo demon Mahiṣāsura (Mahiṣamardinī form) — one of the most iconic images of the goddess in Hindu iconography. The multi-armed goddess is shown triumphing over the demon, symbolising the victory of good over evil.

Artifact_Name: Nṛtta Gaṇapati
Description: Dancing form of Gaṇeśa (Nṛtta Gaṇapati — 'dancing elephant lord'), the elephant-headed deity and remover of obstacles. This dynamic dancing posture is less common than the standard seated Gaṇeśa image.

Artifact_Name: Kārttikeya (seated)
Description: Kārttikeya (also Skanda or Murugan), the Hindu god of war and son of Śiva and Pārvatī, depicted in a seated posture with his peacock vehicle (mayūra). Found in West Dinajpur, India.

Artifact_Name: Navamātrkā
Description: The nine mother goddesses (Navamātrkā) depicted in a single panel — Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahākālī. A major subject in Hindu tantric worship.

Artifact_Name: Manasā
Finding_Place: Tapan, West Dinajpur, West Bengal, India
Description: Manasā, the serpent goddess of Bengal, worshipped primarily for protection against snakebites. She is depicted surrounded by serpents and is a major folk deity of the Bengal region. Found in West Dinajpur, India.

Artifact_Name: Khasarpana (Seated)
Description: Khasarpana Lokeśvara, a compassionate form of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, seated in lalitāsana (royal ease posture). The name means 'one who rescues from the sky/void'. A significant Pāla-period Buddhist image.

Artifact_Name: Kŗṣṅa Yamārī (Halahala Lokesvara)
Description: Kŗṣṅa Yamārī ('the black slayer of Yama'), also identified as Halahala Lokeśvara, a wrathful Vajrayana Buddhist deity. This fierce deity subdues Yama, the god of death, representing triumph over mortality.

Artifact_Name: Head of A Bodhisattva
Description: A finely carved head of a Bodhisattva showing serene facial features characteristic of late Pāla sculptural style — elongated eyes, faint smile, and a high ushnisha (cranial protuberance). Possibly Avalokiteśvara.

Artifact_Name: Mārīcī
Description: An earlier (10th century) depiction of Mārīcī, the Buddhist deity of dawn, with multiple arms and faces. This Vikrampur example differs stylistically from the 11th century Rajshahi version (VRM No. 141), reflecting regional variations.

Artifact_Name: Pārvatī/Umā
Description: Pārvatī or Umā, the consort of Śiva, depicted as a graceful standing female figure in tribhaṅga posture. She holds a lotus and her other hand is in varada mudrā (gift-giving gesture). A fine example of late Pāla female imagery.

Artifact_Name: Mother and Child
Description: A tender sculptural depiction of a mother nursing or cradling a child — a secular theme rarely found in temple sculptures of the period. Reflects the humanistic strand of Pāla-period art alongside religious iconography.

Artifact_Name: Sugatisandarśana Lokeśvara
Description: Sugatisandarśana Lokeśvara ('the Lord who shows the path to blissful rebirth'), a form of Avalokiteśvara that guides sentient beings toward a fortunate rebirth. An important late Pāla Buddhist sculptural subject.

Artifact_Name: Mahattarī Tārā
Description: Mahattarī Tārā ('the great elder Tārā'), a senior or 'great' form of the goddess Tārā, an important female deity in Vajrayana Buddhism. Depicted seated with multiple arms holding various ritual implements.

Artifact_Name: The Triad (Brahma, Viṣṇu and Śiva)
Description: The Hindu Trinity (Trimūrti): Brahmā the creator, Viṣṇu the preserver, and Śiva the destroyer, depicted together in a single sculptural panel. This iconographic form represents the three fundamental cosmic functions in Hindu theology.

Artifact_Name: Śiva:Aghora-Rudra
Description: The fearsome Aghora-Rudra face/manifestation of Śiva, representing his destructive and terrifying aspect. Aghora is one of the five faces of the Pañcamukha Śiva and is associated with the southern direction.

Artifact_Name: Cuṇḍā
Description: Cuṇḍā, a Buddhist goddess associated with auspiciousness, long life, and protection. She is depicted with multiple arms holding various implements and is venerated in both Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhist traditions.

Artifact_Name: Brahmā
Description: Brahmā, the Hindu god of creation and first of the Trimūrti, depicted with his four faces (caturmukha) symbolising the four Vedas and four cardinal directions. He holds a water pot (kamaṇḍalu) and rosary (akṣamālā).

Artifact_Name: Jambhala (Seated)
Description: Jambhala (Kubera in Hindu tradition), the Buddhist god of wealth and abundance, depicted seated with a mongoose (nakula) in one hand and a citron fruit (bijapūra) in the other. The mongoose spits out jewels, symbolising generosity.

Artifact_Name: Vaiṣṇavī
Description: Vaiṣṇavī, one of the Saptamātrkā (seven mother goddesses), the śakti (feminine power) of Viṣṇu. She is depicted with the same iconographic attributes as Viṣṇu, including the discus (cakra) and conch (śaṅkha).

Artifact_Name: Umā-Maheśvara
Description: Umā-Maheśvara — Śiva and his consort Pārvatī (Umā) depicted together in a domestic scene, seated on Mount Kailāsa. This iconographic theme celebrates the divine couple and the harmonious union of masculine and feminine cosmic principles.

Artifact_Name: Siva Nataraja
Description: Śiva as Naṭarāja ('Lord of Dance'), performing the Āṇanda Tāṇḍava cosmic dance. The image encapsulates the cyclical nature of creation, preservation, and destruction, with Śiva trampling the demon Apasmāra (ignorance).

Artifact_Name: Durga Simhavahini
Description: Durgā Siṃhavāhinī ('Durgā who rides the lion') — the goddess in her powerful multi-armed form mounted on her lion vehicle. An important Śākta iconographic subject representing the supreme power of the divine feminine.

Artifact_Name: Viṣṇu
Description: Viṣṇu, the preserver deity of the Hindu Trimūrti, depicted in a standing posture with four arms holding his characteristic attributes: conch (śaṅkha), discus (cakra), mace (gadā), and lotus (padma).

Artifact_Name: Viṣṇu Trivikrama
Description: Viṣṇu as Trivikrama, the 'three-strides' dwarf avatāra (Vāmana), depicting his cosmic stride that covered earth, sky, and heaven in three steps. This image commemorates the defeat of the demon king Bali. Confiscated from customs.

Artifact_Name: Rājbhitā Stone Inscription of Mahipāla the 1st
Description: A stone inscription dated 1010 CE from the reign of Mahipāla I, one of the most powerful rulers of the Pāla dynasty. A key historical document providing information on Pāla administration, land grants, and religious patronage.

Artifact_Name: Bāghbari Inscription of Lakṣmaṇa Sena
Description: A stone inscription from the reign of Lakṣmaṇa Sena (1178–1206 CE), the last major ruler of the Sena dynasty of Bengal, dated 1184–85 CE. An important primary source for the political and religious history of late Sena Bengal.

Artifact_Name: Durgā Siṃhavāhinī
Description: A later Durgā Siṃhavāhinī sculpture from the transitional period between Pāla rule and Sultanate rule (late 12th to early 13th century). Confiscated by customs authorities at Rajshahi and transferred to the museum.

Artifact_Name: Viṣṇu Śrīdhara (inscribed)
Description: Viṣṇu in his Śrīdhara ('bearer of Śrī/Lakṣmī') form, holding a lotus in the lower right hand. This image bears an inscription providing valuable historical information about its origin or patron. Confiscated from customs.

Artifact_Name: Varāhī
