The Kushtia-Rajshahi zone has a significant tradition of silk weaving, and the Jamdani tradition of fine cotton weaving has practitioners in the region. The textile samples displayed include both everyday cotton fabrics and more elaborate woven pieces, showing the range of the district's weaving tradition. The collection is displayed alongside information on the social organization of weaving communities and the impact of industrial textile production on traditional handloom weavers.

Artifact_Name: Liberation War Documents — Kushtia Sector
Provenance_Note: Donated by freedom fighters and families
Description: A collection of Liberation War artifacts and documents from Kushtia District. Kushtia has a notable place in the history of the Liberation War: it was one of the first places where Bangladesh Radio broadcast the independence declaration (from Kalurghat, though also relayed from Kushtia area), and the freedom fighters of the Kushtia-Jhenaidah area fought significant early actions against the Pakistani Army. The collection includes photographs of local freedom fighters, documents relating to liberation activities in the district, and personal effects of martyrs. The display is presented as a tribute to the freedom fighters of Kushtia and contextualizes the district's contribution to national independence.

Artifact_Name: Traditional Household Objects — Kushtia Rural Life
Description: Traditional household objects from the rural villages of Kushtia District, including brass cooking vessels (handi, karahi), clay water pots (kalshi), bamboo grain storage containers (dhamer bhar), and wooden kitchen implements. These everyday objects represent the material culture of Bengali village life in the Kushtia region — the tools and vessels used for cooking, water storage, and food preparation in a typical rural household. The collection serves as a material history of domestic life in Kushtia, complementing the more famous cultural legacy of Lalon Shah and Kangal Harinath with a record of ordinary everyday life in the district.

Artifact_Name: Mughal Miniature Paintings — Lalbagh Collection
Description: A collection of Mughal miniature paintings displayed in the Lalbagh Fort — the museum housed in the Hammam (bathhouse / bathing palace) attached to the Diwan-i-Aam of the fort. The paintings include court scenes, hunting scenes, and portrait studies in the Mughal painting tradition. Mughal miniature painting reached Bengal during the reign of Aurangzeb and his governors in Dhaka; the paintings displayed at Lalbagh represent the artistic culture of the court that built and occupied the fort. The Lalbagh Fort is described as housing Mughal-era artifacts including miniature paintings alongside coins, carpets, calligraphy, swords, and firearms.

Artifact_Name: Mughal Calligraphy Panels
Description: Calligraphy panels in the Mughal tradition displayed in the Lalbagh Fort. The panels feature Arabic and Persian text in various calligraphic styles — naskh, nasta'liq, and thuluth — including Quranic verses, religious phrases, and possibly poetic verses. Calligraphy was the highest art form in the Islamic tradition, and Mughal governors and nobles patronized master calligraphers whose work decorated court buildings and movable artworks alike. The calligraphy panels at Lalbagh provide evidence of the artistic and literary culture of the 17th-century Mughal court in Bengal and complement the architectural calligraphy found on the Pari Bibi tomb within the fort complex.

Artifact_Name: Mughal Swords and Firearms — Arms Collection
Description: A collection of Mughal-period swords and firearms displayed in the Lalbagh Fort. The swords include straight double-edged swords and curved single-edged swords (shamshir) of the Mughal cavalry type, with steel blades and hilts of iron or brass. The firearms include a flintlock musket and a matchlock pistol of the type carried by Mughal infantry and cavalry in the 17th–18th centuries. These weapons represent the military power of the Mughal governors of Bengal who built and occupied Lalbagh Fort. The fort was constructed by Prince Muhammad Azam (later Emperor) from 1678 during his governorship of Bengal, as a royal residence and administrative complex; military equipment was an essential element of such a compound.

Artifact_Name: Mughal Coins — Bengal Mint Series
Description: Mughal coins from the Dhaka (Jahangirnagar) mint, displayed as numismatic evidence of Dhaka's importance as the Mughal provincial capital of Bengal. The coins bear the mint name 'Dar-ul-zarb Jahangirnagar' — confirming Dhaka's role as a major coin-producing center. Silver rupees, gold mohurs, and copper falus from the Aurangzeb period (1658–1707 CE) are the most relevant to the fort's construction period. These coins were the currency of the city that surrounded Lalbagh Fort and of the fort's own garrison and administration. The numismatic collection provides a direct material link to the economic life of 17th-century Dhaka.

Artifact_Name: Pari Bibi Tomb Documentation — Architectural Survey
Description: Documentation and material samples relating to the Tomb of Pari Bibi (Bibi Pari) — the most architecturally significant structure within the Lalbagh Fort complex and one of the finest examples of Mughal architecture in Bangladesh. Pari Bibi was the daughter of Shaista Khan (the Mughal Subahdar of Bengal after Prince Azam's departure) and the fiancée of Prince Azam; she died during construction of the fort, and her death caused Shaista Khan to consider the fort inauspicious and abandon its completion. The tomb is a square structure with white marble cladding, black basalt detailing, and glazed tile mosaic floors. Material samples from the tomb — including marble and tile fragments — are displayed alongside photographs and architectural drawings.

Artifact_Name: Mughal-Era Pottery and Ceramics
Description: Pottery and ceramic artifacts recovered from excavations within the Lalbagh Fort compound, including glazed earthenware bowls and Chinese-import celadon-type pieces that reflect the cosmopolitan material culture of the Mughal court in 17th-century Dhaka. The fort's occupation period (from 1678 onward) is well-documented by pottery, which provides evidence for the use of the different spaces within the fort complex. Chinese porcelain was imported to the Mughal court of Bengal in large quantities; fragments of these prestigious wares found in fort excavations confirm the elevated social status of the compound's inhabitants. The pottery collection complements the architectural and artifact displays in the museum.

Artifact_Name: Mughal Textile Fragments — Carpet and Fabric
Description: Textile fragments including a carpet fragment and silk fabric samples from the Mughal period, displayed as evidence of the luxurious material culture of the Mughal court in Bengal. Mughal carpets — woven in Persia, Central Asia, and later in imperial Indian workshops — were essential furnishings of Mughal royal and administrative buildings. The Diwan-i-Aam (Hall of Public Audience) at Lalbagh Fort, where the governor held public court, would have been furnished with carpets and fine textiles. The fragments displayed provide evidence of the textile culture of the 17th-century Mughal court in Dhaka and complement the miniature paintings and calligraphy in presenting a picture of the court's artistic life.

Artifact_Name: Hammam (Bathhouse) Architecture Documentation
Description: Documentation of the Hammam (Turkish-style bathhouse) that houses the Lalbagh Fort — described as 'the only structure within Lalbagh Fort that is fully accessible to visitors.' The Hammam is a single-storied structure attached to the west of the Diwan-i-Aam, built in the Mughal period as a private bathing facility for the governor and court. It features the characteristic Mughal hammam layout with heated floors (through a hypocaust system), a dressing room, and bathing chambers. Documentation includes measured drawings of the floor plan, photographs of the interior before and after conservation, and samples of the original tile and plaster finishes. The Hammam is a rare surviving example of Mughal domestic architecture in Bangladesh.

Artifact_Name: Fort Construction History Display — Prince Muhammad Azam
Description: An educational display documenting the construction history of Lalbagh Fort — begun in 1678 CE by Prince Muhammad Azam, son of Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb, during his governorship of Bengal. The fort (also known as Fort Aurangabad) was intended to be a royal residence and administrative complex but was left unfinished when Azam was recalled to the Deccan by his father. His successor Shaista Khan abandoned the project after the death of his daughter Pari Bibi, considering the fort inauspicious. The display includes maps of the fort's layout, architectural plans, photographs of all major structures (Diwan-i-Aam, Pari Bibi's Tomb, the Three-Domed Mosque), and a timeline of the fort's construction and subsequent history as a protected monument.

Artifact_Name: Shaista Khan Administration Documents (Replica)
Description: Replica documents from the governorship of Shaista Khan (1664–1688) — the most celebrated of the Mughal Subahdars of Bengal and the administrator who continued work at Lalbagh Fort after Prince Azam's departure. Shaista Khan's governorship is remembered as a golden age for Dhaka: he reportedly reduced the price of rice to such a low level that it became a proverb ('Shaista Khaner amol' — the age of Shaista Khan — means a time of prosperity). He also built the Choto Katra caravanserai, the Sat Gambuj Mosque, and extended Dhaka's defenses. The documents include facsimiles of imperial farmans (orders), revenue records, and correspondence that illuminate the administration of Mughal Bengal from Dhaka.

Artifact_Name: Eternal Flame (Shikha Chirantan) — Entrance Monument
Period_Dating: Established 1996 CE (original site); relocated to new building
Finding_Place: Liberation War Museum entrance, Agargaon, Dhaka
Description: The Eternal Flame (Shikha Chirantan) burns continuously at the entrance of the Liberation War Museum, accompanied by a stone inscription bearing the museum's founding vow: 'In the name of the moon and sun on the sky, in the name of the blood-stained soil of Bengal, we vow not to forget any of our martyrs, any event of our history.' The flame is the symbolic threshold of the museum, marking the transition from ordinary city life into the solemn commemorative space dedicated to the approximately three million people who died and the untold numbers who suffered during the nine-month Liberation War of 1971. It has burned continuously since the museum's original 1996 inauguration at Segunbagicha.

Artifact_Name: Gallery of Heroes — Martyred Intellectuals Exhibit
Finding_Place: Various locations, Dhaka and across Bangladesh
Provenance_Note: Donated by families of martyred intellectuals
Description: An exhibit dedicated to the Martyred Intellectuals of 1971 — the systematic killing of Bengali doctors, professors, writers, journalists, and other intellectuals carried out by the Pakistani Army and local collaborators (Al-Badr militia) in the final days of the war, most notoriously on 14 December 1971, just two days before the surrender. The exhibit displays photographs, personal belongings, and biographical documents of murdered intellectuals, presenting this targeted intellectual genocide as a calculated attempt to cripple the new nation's leadership capacity. The 'Gallery of Heroes' is among the most emotionally powerful and frequently cited sections of the museum by visitors.

Artifact_Name: Original Declaration of Independence Documents
Provenance_Note: Liberation War Museum Trust / government archives
Description: Documents and materials relating to the Declaration of Independence of Bangladesh, proclaimed on 26 March 1971 following the Pakistani Army's crackdown (Operation Searchlight) launched the previous night. The collection includes materials relating to Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's declaration and Major Ziaur Rahman's radio broadcast of the declaration from the Kalurghat radio transmission center near Chittagong. These documents mark the formal beginning of Bangladesh's nine-month armed struggle for independence and are among the most historically significant items in the museum's collection of over 21,000 artifacts.

Artifact_Name: Genocide Documentation — 25 March 1971 (Operation Searchlight)
Finding_Place: Dhaka (University of Dhaka, Old Dhaka, Rajarbagh)
Provenance_Note: Liberation War Museum Trust / journalist and survivor donations
Description: Photographic and documentary evidence of the genocide launched by the Pakistani Army on the night of 25 March 1971 under the codename Operation Searchlight, which targeted the University of Dhaka (killing students and faculty including at Jagannath Hall and Iqbal Hall), the Rajarbagh Police Line, and predominantly Hindu neighborhoods of Old Dhaka. The exhibit presents photographs taken by journalists who managed to document the attacks, newspaper reports from the period, and survivor testimonies. This material forms the evidentiary foundation for understanding the scale and systematic nature of the violence that triggered the full Liberation War.

Artifact_Name: Refugee Crisis Photographs — 1971 Exodus to India
Finding_Place: Border regions, India-Bangladesh frontier and refugee camps
Description: Photographs documenting the massive refugee crisis of 1971, in which an estimated 10 million Bengalis fled across the border into India to escape the violence of the war, creating one of the largest refugee movements in modern history. The images show refugee columns on roads, makeshift camps in West Bengal, Tripura, and Assam, and the humanitarian response from international organizations and the Indian government. This refugee crisis became a major factor in galvanizing international attention and eventually Indian military intervention in December 1971, contributing directly to Bangladesh's liberation.

Artifact_Name: Weapons of the Liberation War — Mukti Bahini Arms
Provenance_Note: Donated by veteran freedom fighters and their families
Description: A collection of weapons used by the Mukti Bahini (the Bangladeshi guerrilla and regular forces) during the Liberation War, including rifles, grenades, and improvised weapons used by the resistance forces who fought a combination of guerrilla and conventional warfare against the Pakistani Army across the nine sectors of the war. The weapons are displayed alongside maps of the sector organization of the resistance and information on the formation and command structure of the Mukti Bahini, which grew from scattered initial resistance by EPR and Bengal Regiment defectors into an organized force that, with Indian military support, achieved victory in December 1971.

Artifact_Name: Personal Belongings of Freedom Fighters and Victims
Provenance_Note: Donated by families of freedom fighters and war victims
Description: Personal belongings of freedom fighters and victims of the 1971 war, including clothing, identification cards, letters, and personal effects, collected through the museum's crowd-funded, citizen-led collection effort since its founding. As 'the outcome of a citizens' effort,' the museum has relied on the general public coming forward with artifacts, including personal belongings and even human remains, to build its collection of more than 21,000 items. These deeply personal objects humanize the statistical scale of the war's casualties (estimated at up to three million deaths) by connecting visitors to specific individuals and families affected by the conflict.

Artifact_Name: Surrender Document Facsimile — 16 December 1971
Finding_Place: Race Course Ground (now Suhrawardy Udyan), Dhaka
Provenance_Note: Liberation War Museum Trust / government archives
Description: A facsimile of the Instrument of Surrender signed on 16 December 1971 at the Race Course Ground in Dhaka, by which Lieutenant General A. A. K. Niazi of the Pakistani Eastern Command surrendered to the Joint Command of Bangladesh and Indian forces under Lieutenant General Jagjit Singh Aurora. This document marks the formal end of the nine-month Liberation War and the birth of independent Bangladesh. The surrender is commemorated annually as Victory Day (Bijoy Dibosh) on 16 December, and its documentation forms the climactic conclusion to the museum's chronological gallery sequence, which begins with Bengali heritage and colonial-era resistance and ends with this moment of national triumph.

Artifact_Name: Pre-1971 Heritage Gallery — Bengali Resistance to British Rule
Description: Materials from the museum's first gallery, which exhibits the heritage of the Bengali people and their historical struggle against British colonial rule, providing essential historical context for the 1971 war. This gallery situates the Liberation War within a longer narrative of Bengali political resistance, beginning with opposition to British rule and continuing through the partition of 1947 and the subsequent grievances under Pakistani rule (1947–1971) documented in Gallery 2. By beginning the museum's narrative arc more than two centuries before 1971, the curators position the Liberation War as the culmination of a long historical process of Bengali political self-assertion.

Artifact_Name: Library and Study Center Archive — War Documentation
Provenance_Note: Liberation War Museum Trust research program
Description: The Liberation War Museum's library and study center, containing books, magazines, periodicals, and other research materials about the Bangladesh Liberation War and the broader history of Bangladesh. The library supports the museum's educational mission and serves researchers, students, and the general public seeking deeper engagement with the war's history beyond the exhibition galleries. The museum also operates a mobile mini-museum that travels to schools across different regions of Bangladesh, extending its educational reach to communities and young people who may not be able to visit the Dhaka facility, fulfilling the institution's mission to ensure that the memory of the Liberation War is transmitted to future generations.

Artifact_Name: Nakshi Kantha — Embroidered Quilt (Lokayon Collection)
Description: A nakshi kantha from the Lokayon Museum collection — one of the museum's examples of Bangladesh's most celebrated folk textile art. The word 'lokayon' itself means 'folk world' or 'folk culture' in Bengali, and the museum's mission is the systematic collection and preservation of objects from the material culture of ordinary Bengali life. This kantha exemplifies that mission: a quilt made from old sari cloth by a rural woman, transformed through embroidery into a work of art. The patterns include a central sun motif surrounded by floral and animal borders. Lokayon Museum collects folk objects that would otherwise be discarded or lost, preserving the creative heritage of ordinary people alongside the monumental heritage of elite culture.

Artifact_Name: Folk Pottery — Kumor Community Collection
Provenance_Note: Donated by kumor (potter) communities / museum field collection
Description: A collection of folk pottery from the kumor (potter) communities of Bangladesh, including ritual objects (mangal ghat — auspicious water pots, Lakshmi and Shiva figurines), household vessels (kalshi, handi, patil), and decorative pieces (painted clay horses and elephants). The kumor caste has been producing pottery in Bengal for thousands of years, maintaining techniques and forms with ancient continuity while adapting to changing markets and tastes. Lokayon Museum's pottery collection represents multiple regional traditions: the red-washed pottery of Comilla, the black pottery of Rajshahi, and the white-painted pieces of Sylhet. The collection documents a craft tradition under severe economic pressure from factory-made alternatives.

Artifact_Name: Rickshaw and Transport Art Collection
Finding_Place: Dhaka and other cities of Bangladesh
Description: A collection of decorated transport objects representing Bangladesh's unique tradition of painted and decorated public vehicles, including rickshaw back panels, hand-pulled cart decorations, and cycle van adornments. Rickshaw art is Bangladesh's most distinctive urban folk art form, transforming functional vehicles into mobile artworks through bright enamel painting, tinsel decorations, and narrative imagery. The collection includes panels depicting landscapes, animals, film stars, historical events, and religious imagery. Lokayon Museum collects rickshaw art as a legitimate and important folk art tradition that captures the intersection of urban culture, folk imagery, and popular aesthetics in Bangladesh's cities.

Artifact_Name: Agricultural and Domestic Tools — Rural Life Collection
Provenance_Note: Museum field collection from rural Bangladesh
Description: A comprehensive collection of agricultural and domestic tools representing the material culture of rural life in Bangladesh, including wooden ploughs (hal), iron sickles (kaste), bamboo winnowing trays (kula), paddy-husking mortars (dheki), spinning wheels (chakra), and weaving implements. These are the tools of everyday life and labor in the Bengali village — the instruments with which rice was grown and processed, cloth was woven, and households were maintained. The Lokayon Museum collects these 'ordinary' objects with the same care as more prestigious art objects, recognizing that the history of ordinary people is as important as the history of kings and aristocrats.

Artifact_Name: Traditional Games and Toys — Children's Folk Culture
Description: A collection of traditional children's games and toys from rural and urban Bangladesh, including clay dolls (mati putul), wooden spinning tops (lattu), bamboo kites (ghuri), marbles (golok), a bamboo hobby horse, and cloth rag dolls. Traditional Bengali children's toys are a significant but often overlooked category of folk craft, made by parents and toy-makers using locally available materials. The collection documents the play culture of Bengali children before the dominance of plastic factory toys and preserves evidence of the skills and imagination involved in handmade toy production. Several of the toys are associated with specific festivals — kites with Sakrain, marbles with the monsoon season.

Artifact_Name: Fishing Equipment — Inland Water Folk Culture
Provenance_Note: Donated by fishing communities / museum field collection
Description: Traditional fishing equipment from the inland water fishing communities of Bangladesh, including a polo (conical bamboo trap), a chaluni (cylindrical wicker trap), a bana (bamboo basket trap), a jhaki jal (cast net), and a traditional baited line. Bangladesh's extensive network of rivers, haors, beels, and floodplains supports a vast inland fishing tradition, and the tools used are adapted to the specific conditions of each water body. The Lokayon Museum collects fishing equipment as evidence of the traditional ecological knowledge of Bangladesh's fishing communities — knowledge that is increasingly under threat from overfishing and habitat loss.

Artifact_Name: Folk Music and Performance Artifacts
Provenance_Note: Donated by folk artists / museum field collection
Description: Traditional folk musical instruments and performance artifacts from Bangladesh's diverse folk music traditions, including instruments associated with jatra (folk theater), kirtan (devotional music), baul (mystic song), and bhatiyali (boatmen's songs). The collection includes a khol (barrel drum for kirtan), a jhanjh (finger cymbals), a sarod-type bowed lute (sarangi), and a bamboo pungi (snake-charmer's instrument). Folk performance is central to the cultural life of rural Bangladesh, marking festivals, life events, and seasonal celebrations. The Lokayon Museum documents these performance traditions as living heritage and collects their material artifacts to preserve evidence of their practice.

Artifact_Name: Traditional Ornaments and Body Decoration
Provenance_Note: Donated by communities / museum field collection
Description: A collection of traditional ornaments and body decoration items from different communities across Bangladesh, including the distinctive conch-shell bangles (shakha) and red lacquer bangles (pola) of Bengali Hindu married women, the glass bangle sets of Muslim women, silver anklets, nose rings of different regional styles, and the shell and bead ornaments of tribal communities. The collection represents the diversity of body adornment traditions across Bangladesh's social and religious communities and documents the craft skills of the specialist artisans — shankhari (conch-shell craftsmen), mali (garland makers), and silver-smiths — who produce these objects. The shakha-pola bangle set is among the most culturally loaded objects in Bengali folk culture, inseparable from the identity of a married Hindu woman.

Artifact_Name: Photograph Album — Mohammad Ali with World Leaders
Description: A bound photograph album documenting Mohammad Ali of Bogra (Mohammad Ali Bogra, 1909–1963) — Prime Minister of Pakistan from 1953 to 1955 — in meetings with world leaders including Queen Elizabeth II, U.S. President John F. Kennedy, and Indian Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru. Mohammad Ali Bogra was the grandson of Nawab Altaf Ali and a member of the prominent Nawab family of Bogra. His premiership came during a critical early period of Pakistani statehood, and his international diplomatic engagements placed Bogra's Nawab family at the center of South Asian and global politics in the 1950s. The album is one of the centerpiece exhibits of the museum, illustrating the family's national and international significance.

Artifact_Name: East India Company Period Coins
Description: A collection of coins dating to the East India Company period (1757–1858), preserved as part of the Nawab family's historical collection at the Palace Museum. The coins include Company-issued sicca rupees and subsidiary copper coinage that circulated in Bengal during the era when the Bogra Nawab family's predecessors were establishing their position as a prominent zamindari and administrative family in northern Bengal. The coin collection reflects the family's nearly two-century continuous presence in Bogra and their participation in the colonial-era economy as substantial landholders and, later, government officials.

Artifact_Name: Antique Firearms — Nawab Family Collection
Description: A collection of antique guns from the Nawab family's historical armory, including flintlock and percussion-cap firearms typical of 19th-century Bengal zamindari households. As a prominent landowning family with administrative responsibilities, the Bogra Nawabs maintained arms for personal security, hunting, and ceremonial display. The firearms collection is displayed in the historic Nawab Palace alongside other artifacts of the family's elite domestic life, illustrating the material culture of a northern Bengal nawabi household across multiple generations leading up to Mohammad Ali Bogra's 20th-century political prominence.

Artifact_Name: Rare Book Collection — 100 Years Old
Description: A collection of rare books, approximately 100 years old, preserved from the personal library of the Bogra Nawab family. The collection includes works of Bengali and English literature, religious texts, and reference works that reflect the educated, cosmopolitan character of the Nawab household. The family's commitment to education and literary culture is reflected in this collection, which provided the intellectual environment in which Mohammad Ali Bogra and other family members were raised before later generations pursued careers in national and international politics, administration, and diplomacy.

Artifact_Name: Nawab Family Costumes and Clothing
Description: A collection of traditional and formal costumes and clothing belonging to members of the Bogra Nawab family, spanning from the late 19th century through Mohammad Ali Bogra's diplomatic career in the mid-20th century. The costumes include formal sherwanis, ceremonial robes, and items of Western-style formal dress worn for state occasions and diplomatic functions. The clothing collection documents the sartorial evolution of an elite Bengali Muslim family across the transition from colonial-era zamindari status to post-independence national political leadership, reflecting both Islamic cultural traditions and the cosmopolitan, internationally engaged identity of the later generations.

Artifact_Name: Terracotta Decorative Panels — Palace Architecture
Description: Well-decorated terracotta panels from the architectural fabric of the Nawab Palace, the historic two-storied building constructed on the western bank of the Karatoya River that now houses the Mohammad Ali Palace Museum. The palace building, over 180 years old, has eight rooms and nine doors on its upper floor and sixteen rooms and thirteen doors on the ground floor. The terracotta decoration reflects the architectural ambitions of the Nawab family in establishing their residence as a landmark of Bogra city. The palace was officially declared a Preserved Antiquity by the Department of Archaeology in May 2016, recognizing its historical and architectural significance.

Artifact_Name: Sculptures by Aminul Karim Dulal
Description: Sculptures created by the prominent Bangladeshi artist Aminul Karim Dulal, who designed several statues and structures now on display at the Palace Museum, including paper-made eye-catching statues described as among the museum's notable attractions. One room of the museum has been specially decorated with paintings of Nawab family members alongside Dulal's sculptural works. This combination of family portraiture and contemporary sculptural art reflects the museum's dual mission: preserving the specific history of the Nawab family of Bogra while also serving as a venue for Bangladeshi artistic expression and a cultural attraction for the wider public, especially young visitors learning about regional history.

Artifact_Name: Family Portrait Paintings — Nawab Lineage
Description: A series of portrait paintings depicting members of the Nawab family of Bogra across multiple generations, displayed in a dedicated room of the Palace Museum. The portraits trace the family lineage from Nawab Altaf Ali through to Mohammad Ali Bogra, documenting the family's evolution from regional zamindari aristocracy to national political leadership. The 180-year-old Nawab Palace itself is dedicated to the memory of both Mohammad Ali and the broader Nawab family, who are remembered for contributions to improving local living conditions in the Bogra region. The portrait gallery provides visual continuity to the family's multi-generational story alongside the documentary photographs and personal artifacts displayed elsewhere in the museum.

Artifact_Name: Furniture Collection — Nawab Palace Interiors
Description: Furniture preserved from the original interiors of the Nawab Palace, including pieces from the family's reception rooms and private quarters. The furniture reflects the domestic material culture of a wealthy northern Bengal Muslim aristocratic household across the late colonial and early independence periods. As the largest family museum in northern Bangladesh, the Palace Museum places particular emphasis on these domestic artifacts to give visitors — especially the young students who form a large part of the museum's visitorship — a tangible sense of how the Nawab family lived, distinct from the more abstract political history represented by the photographs and documents elsewhere in the collection.

Artifact_Name: Nawab Family Graves and Memorial Site Documentation
Provenance_Note: Department of Archaeology / Bogra District administration
Description: Documentation of the graves of Nawab family members located within the Palace Museum grounds, which include the palace, an amusement park, a market, and the family burial site. Photographs and site plans document the location and inscriptions of the family graves, providing genealogical and historical information that complements the indoor exhibits. The park surrounding the palace, with its seventy-one trees and three ornamental gateways (including one with a clock and searchlight), forms an integrated heritage landscape with the museum buildings, all situated on the eastern bank of the Karatoya River near Satmatha — the historic commercial center of Bogra city.

Artifact_Name: Portrait of Munshi Abdur Rouf (Birshreshtha)
Provenance_Note: Bangladesh National Museum / Liberation War archives
Description: A formal portrait of Lance Nayek Munshi Abdur Rouf (8 May 1943 – 20 April 1971), recipient of Bangladesh's highest military honor, Bir Sreshtho, for his extraordinary bravery during the Liberation War of 1971. Abdur Rouf served in the 11th Wing of the East Pakistan Rifles and died on 20 April 1971 at Burighat in the Chittagong Hill Tracts, holding back Pakistani Army forces with his machine gun until he was killed, enabling his comrades to retreat to safety. Born in Salamatpur (now Roufnagar) in Faridpur, he is one of only seven freedom fighters awarded the Bir Sreshtho — the nation's highest gallantry award. The portrait is the central exhibit of the museum, placed at the entrance where all visitors pass.

Artifact_Name: Military Uniform and Insignia (Replica)
Provenance_Note: Bangladesh Border Guard / Liberation War archives
Description: A replica of the East Pakistan Rifles (EPR) uniform and insignia of the type worn by Lance Nayek Munshi Abdur Rouf during the 1971 Liberation War. The uniform consists of the standard khaki EPR field dress with the rank insignia of Lance Nayek (one stripe) on the sleeve. The EPR (now the Border Guard Bangladesh / BGB) was the paramilitary force in which Rouf served. On 25–26 March 1971, when the Pakistani Army launched Operation Searchlight, EPR soldiers like Rouf joined the resistance immediately, forming the backbone of the early guerrilla forces of Sector 1. The uniform is displayed alongside a map showing the Chittagong Hill Tracts theater of operations where Rouf fought and died.

Artifact_Name: Machine Gun (LMG) — Type Used by Abdur Rouf (Replica)
Finding_Place: Liberation War theater, Chittagong Hill Tracts
Provenance_Note: Bangladesh Army / Liberation War Museum archives
Description: A deactivated replica of the Light Machine Gun (LMG) of the type used by Lance Nayek Munshi Abdur Rouf in his final battle at Burighat on 20 April 1971. According to Liberation War records, Rouf single-handedly manned his LMG post against a Pakistani Army assault, continuing to fire even after he was wounded, enabling his sector to hold and his comrades to reach safety. He died at his post. The LMG display is accompanied by a detailed narrative of the Burighat battle and the tactical context of Sector 1 operations in the Chittagong Hill Tracts during April 1971. This exhibit is the most emotionally charged in the museum.

Artifact_Name: Bir Sreshtho Award Citation and Medal (Replica)
Description: A replica of the Bir Sreshtho citation and gallantry medal — Bangladesh's highest military honor — awarded posthumously to Munshi Abdur Rouf by the Government of Bangladesh. The Bir Sreshtho (Supreme Hero) is the highest of Bangladesh's six valour awards, given for the most conspicuous bravery. Only seven freedom fighters received it during the 1971 Liberation War; all seven are now celebrated as national heroes. The citation documents Rouf's specific act of bravery at Burighat. The original medal and citation are held by the family; the museum displays a high-quality replica alongside the official gazette notification of the award. A panel explains the Bir Sreshtho award system and profiles all seven recipients.

Artifact_Name: Photographs — Liberation War Sector 1 Operations
Provenance_Note: Liberation War archives / donated by sector veterans
Description: A collection of photographs documenting the operations of Sector 1 of the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War — the sector in which Munshi Abdur Rouf served and died. The photographs include images of EPR guerrilla fighters, the landscape of the Chittagong Hill Tracts theater, and Liberation War memorial sites. Sector 1 covered the Chittagong and Hill Tracts region and was commanded by Major Ziaur Rahman (later President of Bangladesh) in the early weeks of the war. The photographs are displayed with detailed captions tracing the military history of the sector and contextualizing Rouf's sacrifice within the broader liberation struggle.

Artifact_Name: Mother's Testimony — Mokidunnesa (Recorded Document)
Description: A printed record and digitized audio recording of the testimony of Mokidunnesa — the mother of Munshi Abdur Rouf — given at the museum's inauguration ceremony on 28 May 2008. Mokidunnesa attended the inauguration as a special guest and spoke about her son's childhood, his service in the EPR, and the news of his death. Her account is one of the most direct personal testimonies relating to any of the seven Bir Sreshtho recipients and provides a human dimension to the heroic narrative. The document is displayed alongside a photograph of the inauguration ceremony showing Mokidunnesa with government officials. Her presence at the opening was one of the most moving moments in the museum's history.

Artifact_Name: Village History Display — Roufnagar (Salamatpur)
Provenance_Note: Faridpur District administration / museum research team
Description: An educational display documenting the history of Roufnagar village (formerly Salamatpur) — the birthplace of Munshi Abdur Rouf — including historical photographs, a map of the area, and text panels on the village's geography, demography, and economy. The display traces the village's history from its colonial-era name Salamatpur through its renaming as Roufnagar in honor of the Bir Sreshtho hero. The village is located in Modhukhali Upazila of Faridpur District on the banks of the Padma River, and the display includes information on the river's influence on the local economy and culture. The museum is positioned very close to the river bank, and river erosion has been a documented threat to the museum building.

Artifact_Name: Liberation War Book Collection — Library
Provenance_Note: Government of Bangladesh; donated by public
Description: The museum's integrated library collection, comprising books on the Bangladesh Liberation War, the seven Bir Sreshtho heroes, military history, the history of Faridpur district, and Bengali literature. The library was established alongside the museum in 2008 as part of the government's initiative to open ten memorial museums in honor of the Bir Sreshtho recipients and language martyrs. The collection includes published memoirs of Liberation War sector commanders, official government publications on the war, biographies of Munshi Abdur Rouf, and a selection of Bengali literature. The library is open to local students and researchers and serves an educational function complementary to the museum's memorial role.

Artifact_Name: Map of Bangladesh Liberation War (1971) — All Sectors
Description: A large wall map of Bangladesh showing the eleven sectors of the 1971 Liberation War, with Sector 1 (Munshi Abdur Rouf's sector, covering Chittagong and Hill Tracts) highlighted. The map shows the major battle sites, guerrilla bases, Pakistani Army positions, and refugee routes. It provides essential geographical context for visitors to understand the strategic situation of the liberation struggle and the specific location of the Burighat battle where Rouf died. The map is accompanied by a timeline of the key events of the war from 25 March to 16 December 1971 and photographs of major liberation war sites across all eleven sectors.

Artifact_Name: Personal Effects — Childhood Artifacts from Roufnagar
Provenance_Note: Donated by Munshi Abdur Rouf family
Description: A small collection of personal effects and childhood artifacts associated with Munshi Abdur Rouf's early life in Roufnagar, donated by his family for the museum collection. The items include a childhood photograph, a school exercise book, and simple household objects from the family home. These personal items humanize the heroic narrative of the museum, showing Abdur Rouf not only as a military hero but as a son, student, and village boy who grew up in ordinary rural circumstances in Faridpur. The display is accompanied by a brief biography tracing Rouf's life from his birth on 8 May 1943 through his enlistment in the EPR on 8 May 1963 (his 20th birthday) to his death at age 27 in 1971.
